It's basically a city builder combined with some god like powers, a snail rush enemy and random disasters in other city builders.

Powers and some tower mechanics are linked to energy. Energy is gained by creatures dying or rubbish being burnt. (Personally I would have thought faith was a better mechanic)

Snail rush enemy seeps over the land, you have no power over enemy land and hence cannot build in those locations or use your powers in those locations.

Building is limited to slots. A slot is taken for each building you create upto a maximum limit. To extend the limit you have to improve your town centre or build an "ancillary". The larger each building gets the more resources are required.

Fire pits take a building slot, cannot be destroyed by the enemy and push back the "Blighted land". Hence the majority of the game is "dance with fire pits".

Towers allow incoming enemies to be killed in various ways. Walls keep enemies at bay but are destroyed by the "Blight" (They burn to nothing).

Due to limited population mechanics you never want to put your people at risk, combat is self defeating.

Unfortunately the game is a conceptually a mess. God energy and tower energy are gained through burning rubbish ? Enemies cannot destroy fire pits ? Enemies have unlimited population ? Enemies continually take land.

The game ends up being a very frustrating and boring city builder. The game is dominated by fire pits and building slots - that's the real game you are playing. Random disasters just make the game a useless waste of time - pressing the reset button on you strategy - it's a very poor excuse for game play and lacks imagination.

Very frustrating. If the developer had used faith as a dynamic pushing between the opposing forces, the player would have to expand or be defeated. Requiring faith to build would have limited the rate of expansion. Losing followers would reduce faith and limit short term game play. The same mechanic could operate for the enemy.

Unfortunately the poor mechanics makes for poor and frustrating game play.

The interface is very hard to see and requires too much detailed hand movements to interact with - icons are way too small.

I'd put this as buyer be ware rather than recommend or stay away. Time Steam put in a third option.

Rise to Ruins is a fantastic town management god-sim tower defense game that can best be described as The Settlers vs. Dungeon Keeper. You play as a benevolent god of some kind that is trying to guide a group of people to a safe future in a world where the dead walk and hate humanity. They will attack in the night, and your villagers will need to be ready with walls, towers, golems, and gates. Your villagers will mostly build, repair, and arm these machines as well as build the necessary infrastructure to do so, as well as gathering their own food and water, and building their own shelter. You, of course, will tell them what to do.

It's a slow-moving game, but I love the relaxing music that plays in the daytime as well as the tense ominousness of night. If you need constant action, this is not for you, but if you ever wished that chill city-building games like Banished could come with a tower defense mod that throws zombies and ghosts at you every night, then this is definitely for you.

It's a frustrating game. When I got it, I was hoping it would be one of those games you can easily sink 100 hours into without getting bored, but now I'm 8 hours in and I don't think it will be. The game doesn't even try to explain itself to you, so you're supposed to learn through trial and error, but the problem with this is that trial and error can only give you a vague sense of what's going on, I'm still left confused about the details of what these buildings actually do or how my villagers will actually do their work. 

Defending against monsters is much easier than just keeping your villagers alive. I always lose due to my villagers starving, never to the monsters. I've seen lots of other reviewers complaining about their villagers starving, so this seems to be a pretty common issue for new players. I think that's a failure of the game to explain the basics of food management to the player. I always build and fully upgrade a farm and a kitchen early on, but that doesn't seem to help since food primarily just spawns in the wild, the farms don't seem to do much, and I'm not really sure what staffing farmers do. Do farmers just collect wild food? If I staff the farm with multiple farmers, will the crops grow faster? How much water is needed in order for farm food to grow? These are the kind of questions that you'll never get answers too in the game, no matter how much trial and error you do. 

I'm still giving it a thumbs up, because I think it's a decent strategy game, it's cheap, and clearly some people out there really enjoy it. Personally I'd give it more of a 5/10 - not bad, not good. If I went through the trouble of looking up how you're supposed to play this game on you tube or something, I would probably enjoy it more, but at the same time I don't like copying strategies from other players, I prefer to find my own way in these types of games, but I can't really do that when there are so many unanswered questions about how the game works.

Rise to Ruins is an exceptional godlike village simulation game that blends the best elements of the god game management, tower defense, and city builder genres. With its similar feel to games like Rimworld and Dwarf Fortress, this indie game offers a unique and thrilling experience that will keep you engaged for hours on end.

The game has a pixel graphics style that is both charming and immersive. The attention to detail in the game's world-building is remarkable, and the game's environments are beautifully crafted. The game's soundtrack is also noteworthy, with a mix of ambient and orchestral music that perfectly captures the game's mood.

The gameplay in Rise to Ruins is harsh but satisfying. As a player, you take on the role of a god who must guide a small village through the dangers of a unforgiving world. You must manage your resources, build structures, and defend your village from hordes of monsters that threaten your survival. The game's tower defense elements are interesting, and the game's survival mechanics are challenging but fair.

One of the things that stand out about Rise to Ruins is the game's depth. There is a vast array of structures, technologies, and resources to manage, and each decision you make has consequences that affect the game's outcome. The game's sandbox elements allow for endless replayability.

Overall, Rise to Ruins is an outstanding game that offers a unique and immersive experience. It's a must-play for fans of the god game management, tower defense, and city building genres. If you're looking for a challenging and rewarding game that will keep you engaged for hours on end, Rise to Ruins is the game for you.

If I had to put the priority of the game types this would be most in alignment with assuming you play it in standard / traditional mode and not "peaceful" mode, it would be sim management, tower defense, city builder, godlike.

Sim management, this is almost I daresay the bread and butter because so many things can go wrong.  You don't just build a population like in many city builders.  You have to wait for either nomads to come along, or wait for your sims to have children, and then grow up before you can use them.  After managing to get some additional sims aside from your starter, you need to keep them alive and manage their task types.  Messing up this part will fundamentally screw you over.

Tower defense comes in a very close second, because at the end of the day (literally each day), monsters come to your base, if you don't protect it and your sims, you won't get far.

City builder comes in third, but also only ever so slightly, because it lays the foundation for the rest of your game.  You need to make sure you upgrade your buildings along the way and not just build like a fanatic because see #1 about sims (you don't have a very big population to work with at the start).

Godlike, comes in last but is surprisingly VERY effective for whatever you need it for.  Whether it is to keep regenerating resources or to spawn new ones, or summoning a temporary golem to keep your base alive, this one covers it all in the forms of utility, offensive, defensive and aiding spells.  Problem is, the only way to keep increase your "mana" is to maintain high population (see again #1, sims).

TLDR:  the game is rather intricate if you take the time to learn it and very rewarding once you get a feel for all the mechanics.  Plays like an old school city builder, but with much more depth.

I've barely played this but I am in love with this game. It mixes a lot of elements I love from other games. 

You have something that's a tower defense, and actually properly built as such, unlike Rimworld, which doesn't seem to want to admit its tower defense nature. 

You have a fantasy village sim, with intricate details like water treatment, garbage, and multiple regions with migration. The production chain is beautiful. It's sort of like an arcade Dwarf Fortress, with the details of equipping all your little guys with bows and armor. There's detail in how buildings work, like how stone is dropped off in different parts of the building, instead of all in one spot. As buildings upgrade, you see even more details appear based on the type of upgrade.

While it's not quite Dwarf Fortress level complexity, it gets across much of the fortress building gameplay, but it's playable much faster than DF and Rimworld. Losing is much of the fun in these games, and Rise to Ruins will also accelerate you to a satisfactory defeat.

There's a tutorial, but it's also paced right in that it doesn't let you drown from complexity, but also doesn't handhold you. For example, I didn't realize that I needed farms to keep my people fed or that wells didn't bring in drinkable water, and it will gently tell me on Day 3 to handle these, giving me plenty of time (and deaths) to figure the game out myself.

EDIT: After playing for 40+ hours I'm rewriting my review for this game.

Rise to Ruins has hints of games about it like Rimworld, Factorio, Terraria, and They Are Billions. In its current state it is rather simplistic featuring a day/night cycle in which you survive building by day and fending off a slow creeping horde of enemies by night. There are some basic tips but the finer details of play you learn the hard way through experiencing defeat giving the game a bit of a learning curve. Once figured out surviving to late game days where the enemies become stronger as you restrict their building area making them significantly more difficult is pretty easy.
From there comes the challenge, most defense tower units are useless even fully upgraded and without a well planned labyrinth for defense you will find even a meager slime can enter your base and begin to ransack all your buildings. Even with hundreds of villagers and plenty of "rangers" to defend your town one monster can just run around killing everyone while destroying everything you have worked toward. The power creep feels incredibly unbalanced even on traditional mode.
The management aspect is a little tedious where sometimes villagers just don't do their prospective job even when there is nothing left for them to do, let me tell you watching a tower sit at 4 rock to complete building/upgrading can be frustrating especially when the building is set to top priority.
That said, Rise to Ruin has a lot of potential for being a consistently updated indie game. The frustration and challenge can feel rewarding while the defeat can be absolutely heart wrenching. If you enjoy games of this genre I would suggest giving it a try, because I believe Rise to Ruins will only get better with time. For the price of the game you will get your money's worth.

Now before you lose your mind, I understand the concept of "endless" content, but this game specifically is capable of having win conditions with how each level can interact with one another. In its current state, you barely get to make use of the world map because you just get wiped on the first level. Each level is designed to go on forever, the "endgame" of each level is essentially a stalemate until the enemy inevitably out-scales you.

Instead, the earlier levels should be "beatable", meaning you can completely wipe out the enemy and have the map to yourself. The cleared maps would then be exclusively used as logistic bases to help fund your "front line" bases. As you advance through the world map, the enemy becomes a little more aggressive and expands a bit faster. Once you get to the last couple maps, the enemy starts to behave like it does now, where it essentially scales infinitely until you get wiped.

Okay to start off, this IS like your average city-builder. 
Even if it's your everyday city-builder, it has a lot of things going for it such as little references to real life people whenever a nomad decides to stay in your land or whenever a child is born to small pieces of text hidden outside the map. 

To mention on of this game's strongest points, actually wouldn't really be the city building in my opinion but it starts at the map editor. Yep, you heard me, the map editor. Whilst I haven't personally used this, from all  the city-builder games I've played in the past only two of them have had the addition of map editing including this game. Which sadly, I haven't seen many maps made by someone else besides good ol' Raymond himself (the maker of Rise To Ruins). 

Next: The city building
It comes to no surprise that this game has a bit of a selection when it comes to city building, from your average "city-builder" housing all the way to even having trash collection and burning to keep your city/village clean. While a lot of the buildings may have a max upgrade that can be somewhat expensive, a lot of the upgrades actually do something. Instead of just being a small little upgrade, such as adding a production boost every upgrade. Which is a flat upgrade to production buildings. You can even build walls and fences for your homes!

The gamemodes
Okay so there are a few gamemodes in Rise to Ruins which include: Nightmare, survival, traditional, peaceful, custom and sandbox.
Obviously, to start off, Nightmare mode. Honestly if you're playing on this gamemode you either have a death wish or just enjoy watching your townsfolk suffer.

Survival coming up next, this was the way the game was intended to be played which it even mentions on the mode's description that there is a big learning steep whilst playing in Survival.

Traditional will probably be the only way I'll play this game for a while until I get a better grip because Traditional is the gamemode meant for people who are new to city-builder games or just in general, new to Rise To Ruins. It offers some challenge to keep you on your toes while also being lenient with how many monsters are actually being sent.

Peaceful mode. My favorite mode. In this mode the name says it all, this goes from Rise To Ruins to Rise to Ruins strict city-builder. This mode offers no challenge besides keeping your townsfolk alive. Definitely a recommendation for those who are looking for the most laid back experience you can get in the game without going full blown sandbox.

Custom mode is a mode I haven't personally tried out yet but just from the name it should be pretty obvious. You can set your own difficulties and game perimeters to play with at your very own custom difficulty.

Now sandbox is just self explanatory. You can screw around whit everything this game has to offer. From changing the time of day to just simply spawning in resources. 100% the gamemode to use if you really just enjoy fucking around with the game mechanincs themselves.

My overall judgement of this game is: I love it. Personally there are a few thing's I'd like to see be done. Some thing's I'd even like to see brought back eventually like the 5x gamespeed. Though this game as it is right now is honestly a blast and is definitely a fun time waster and a genuinely fun game if you're playing it for the challenge. I hope to see a lot from this game in future updates as soon as Raymond is able to! For now though, you all should enjoy your time in this game, whether you're making your townsfolk suffer by spawning a metric fuck ton of volcanoes or spawning in Holy Golems to protect them from the corrupted scum!z

This is hands-down the best [b]indirect control city builder[/b] I have ever played...
...but the current version has some quirks - and [b]a MASSIVE potential deal-breaker[/b] that you might not be able to look past.

[h1]The Pitch[/h1]
Have you wanted to like [i]The Settlers 3[/i] but hated how all that city building just fed into a crummy RTS? Or wished [i]Alien Nations II[/i] didn't have all these dystopian overtones and worked past Windows XP?

Then this is a game for you.

[i]Rise to Ruins[/i] is all about managing a single village by constructing and upgrading [b]buildings, walls and roads[/b], and assigning villagers to [b]jobs[/b], throughout [b]four seasons[/b] of the year and occasional earthquakes, meteor showers, or whatnot.

The main obstacle of the game is dealing with [b]nightly monster waves[/b] - spawning out of the spreading [b]Corruption[/b] - which need to be dealt by a three-part defense of [b]Tower-Defense-style towers[/b], a fully [b]automatic army of golems[/b], and a range of [b]God-Sim-style spells[/b].

All of which is neatly tied up in [b]a campaign[/b] that tasks you with surviving a year on each map of a hand-crafted continent. And there's also [b]skirmish with 5 modes[/b] and [b]a map editor[/b].

[h1]The Good[/h1]
Raymond Doerr [b]"gets it"[/b] when it comes to the genre: rock is renewable (finally!), roads are affordable, the economy is grokkable, and [b]the UI/UX is very functional, efficient, and intuitive[/b] (mostly). And, importantly, the villagers are made of [b]The Sterner Stuff™[/b] but are still too squishy for a functional military. [i]RtR[/i] has the fundamentals right.

And there are many more good things about it: the best [b]trash management[/b] I've ever seen, all towers having a niche, tutorial tips, naming conventions, [b]exhaustive and comprehensive Problems panel[/b]. 

The game requires [b]no quick reflexes[/b], [b]no micromanagement[/b], and [u][b]no advanced spatial imagination[/b][/u] - placing a building 1 tile to the left [i]won't mean[/i] it doesn't get a bonus or works at 12% efficiency.

But most importantly - [i]RtR[/i] is [b]definitely learnable[/b]. Every time I've lost, I had very clear understanding of what the exact chain of reactions led to the massacre of my poor, poor villagers, and plans on how to do it better next time. And then I actually did better!

[h1]The Weird[/h1]
[b]Event log is odd[/b]: it shows destruction of your [i]and Corruption's[/i] buildings, building repairs, villagers [i]literally [b][u]FUCKING[/u][/b][/i] - but not births/[i]miscarriages[/i]/immigrations/deaths, which are only displayed in the middle of the screen for a couple of seconds.

The tower defense element [b]wouldn't stand on its own[/b] - it's not bad to simplify some genre elements in a genre-straddling, but bear in mind that:
[list]
[*]towers have no targetting options nor exploitable priorities,
[*]there are no buff/repair/targetting towers,
[*]the sole crowd control tower "banishes" in a tiny radius, so it [i]miiiight[/i] teleport monsters straight into your undefended areas,
[*]1 out of 3 elemental damage choices is Poison, even though most monsters are resistant to it and [i]no monster is vulnerable to it[/i],
[*]no, seriously, what's up with Poison?
[/list]

And there's some more strangeness. Villagers are easily spooked by you dropping materials into buildings; campaign UI doesn't differentiate between maps beaten with and without the one-year-goal; and I still don't know whether Crystal Golems are worth their tiny HP pool, since only towers have damage estimates.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
Tutorial tips break down when your Very First Village is Inevitably Getting Massacred - which you'd think is the one case that [i]would[/i] be covered by a hard survival game - and [b]don't explain that you're supposed to restart the campaign[/b] now that there are literally no more playable maps.

UI/UX is [b]very good, but requires more polish[/b], since it has problems that are:
[olist]
[*] [b]minor:[/b] all harvest zones are marked by the exact same circles and rings that visually blend together, and the building preview uses yellow both to mean [i]"can't build here because this is inside another building's zone"[/i] and [i]"can build here but villagers will flatten terrain before building"[/i];
[*] [b]major:[/b] the Problems panel and the event log will tell you there's a very location-specific problem, but [b]won't tell you [i]where[/i][/b];
[*] [b]annoying:[/b] once monsters start slaughtering all your villagers, better take off headphones, since [i]"a villager died"[/i] fanfare is about to play for every. Single. One. Of. Your. 125+. Villagers.
[/olist]

And there's also:

[h2]The Potential Deal-Breaker[/h2]
The current update 1C of [i]RtR[/i] is [b]both [i]complete[/i] and [i]incomplete[/i][/b].

On the [b]campaign[/b] level, it is [i]complete[/i] as a game about surviving a year on every map [b]in a single go with no failures[/b]. But it's [i]incomplete[/i] as a game where you can [b]recover from your mistakes[/b]. After failing a single map by a single day - doesn't matter whether it's the first, the third, or the very last, nor whether other maps have smouldering ruins or thriving kingdoms - you need to start the whole campaign over.

On the [b]map[/b] level, it is [i]complete[/i] as a game about as a game about [b]surving a year[/b] - and then, optionally, until your defenses are inevitably overwhelmed. But - even though there are mechanics geared toward that - it's [i]incomplete[/i] as a game about beating Corruption.

The [i]only[/i] way to combat Corruption is with Corruption Resistance (CR), generated in a varying radius around every building. Which works great as an intutive boundary of your village, as means of getting a [i]juuust little bit[/i] of extra room back from Corruption, and is leagues above crummy RTS elements from other games. But as an offensive tool... it's bad.

The main issue stems from the need for efficiency - [b]funnels[/b] you into expanding by [b]building Large Firepits, and Large Firepits only[/b]. Whether you're a first-day pauper, a thriving survivor, or a yearling sitting on a hillariously great economy with all these resources and villagers and space and building slots and spells and mana... Like any game, it's not without its frustrating bits though:

There are quite a few complaints regarding the AI of the villagers, and rightly so.
The prioritising of build projects doesn't seem to do much, builders will walk a long way to work on a project that can't be finished because it's missing 1 piece of wood (which they won't bring with them), organizers will not group projects (multiple projects next to each other that require a single piece of wood will require multiple walks, etc), they never seem to learn they shouldn't fight fire elementals, ...

There is a dialog that does provide you with some info (like monsters attacking a building, villagers being in a fight, ...) but you don't know where it's happening. So you have to check each building if there's a hard-to-see ghost attacking it.

I could go on, but all in all these issues aren't show-stoppers. They're just things you eventually notice and you wish you didn't have to work around.

A fantastic game, with lovely pixel-art graphics, a challenging learning curve, and a pleasant soundtrack to keep company. A solid 7/10 game and beneath is an essay if you're interested

          After all this time I decided to update my review from the original, which I put in the comments below, and it is worth reading as I now have a few things to say about my previous take and concerns, and because I've been playing the unstable beta version which I enjoy even more than the main update.

          Originally I thought I was clever about making use of various exploits but I was shocked to discover that originally these exploits didn't exist!! Updates made the game much easier and made such exploits possible way sooner, even for new accounts

          Expanding on what I mean about exploits, when you make an account you have a world map, and as you play you gain permanent upgrades affecting you villagers and god-powers which is my favorite part of the game, these upgrades are potentially infinite which means exploits are inevitable anyways, but no longer require hundreds of hours to get there, once you learn the game, you can beat the game absolutely.

          Skirmishes are different, and has no relation to your world map or upgrades at all! You simply play one region, and survive as long as possible, but without ways to infinitely expand to keep up with corruption I don't see much fun in it, especially knowing its possible to get a "permanent victory" by completely wiping corruption off the region! Its difficult but possible, and those two reasons together are why I don't enjoy Skirmishes.

          Now I mentioned corruption, which is revealed in the trailer as a dark force that overtakes your region, sending monsters to try and destroy you, but corruption can't expand through your borders, so to defeat corruption you must place and defend a ton of buildings, and it turns out the best building to use for that, are lights, yep just campfire lights, they expand your base size plenty and won't be attacked by monsters, so by playing aggressively you can completely remove corruption within about 10-20 in-game days and then move on to another region.

          10-20 days gets you close to a full in-game year, which is about 28 days, 7 per season, so if you remove the corruption completely you may as well stay for the full year to claim your victory point for your region (unless of course you are doing a Skirmish)

          I'm going to hope for this next part you've read all about the update patches and changes between the stable and unstable versions, because here in my review is where the two really start to deviate, the unstable version changes your god-powers greatly, and increases the importance of having a lot of villagers and treating them well. Your villagers now have Faith, which ONLY affects your god-powers, granting you enough influence (the extent of your magic powers) to cast stronger spells and more spells, Faith allows you to obtain much more influence far quicker and also lose a region much faster, because bad things reduce faith and good things increase faith, you also use Altars where you assign villagers to an occultist job in which they send prayers, spawning essence and increasing faith of all nearby villagers. The god powers themselves are all slightly nerfed to counter this massively increased power potential, and a new expensive spell was added that can be cast after about 100 population with enough faith.

This alone is a massive change to the game as playing aggressively is far more consequential, as even at high faith losing one villager hurts total faith more and can quickly drop you down to being unable to do much at all while your village gets swamped, so you have to time your aggression more carefully and expand a little more slowly.

          I also want to touch on difficulty, I still prefer traditional over the harder difficulties as I enjoy being an overpowered warlord who dominates the map, and harder difficulties only means it takes longer to get to that point, but I want to get OP as fast as possible so a harder game to me just wastes more time.

          The magic is the only change that really matters for the sake of this review essay, but there are a bunch of little changes that I do like, such as essence not always being collectible (when an essence collector is sending to a tower for ex, obv I wouldn't want to steal that) and bodies making a little 'POP' when you click them enough and giving more essence on death in general.

          To compare more with my first review, I learned that fire elementals aren't completely overpowered, if you get them into melee they deal far less damage and don't light things on fire, which means its a good idea to keep some golem machines just one away from max upgrade, so that these golems don't gain a ranged attack.
          I have a better headset now, but if I do unplug on accident the bug I mentioned is still true.
         AI is still embarrassingly dumb, this provides a great opportunity actually, there could be a new stat called intelligence and you could build a school to teach villagers to be more efficient and really expand this game in a whole new way, better pathfinding, more efficient resource delivering, villagers knowing when its okay to stay in combat or to run away, more equipment types et cetera would be great, which brings to the next con -
          Variety, once you get past that learning curve it becomes clear that there really is only one way to play if you want to win, use campfires and golems and funnel the enemies with careful wall placement, god powers are only necessary for helping your villagers live and helping build more defenses and just being helpful in general, there are no additional possible victory conditions than just long term survival and while I was wrong about region variety (there actually is variety and its really obvious by just looking at the red sand maps compared to the forest, there is lava on red sands and more resources in the foresty areas, the black rock map has actual tar that you can't build on, and I haven't checked the others) there still isn't much in terms of gameplay strategy, and I believe more customization, modding ability, and maybe even multiplayer could fix that. I can easily think up great multiplayer ideas as well like having to compete over trying to conquer the same map but different starting regions, or playing against each other instead of corruption which makes Skirmishes way more fun and even makes "attacking" another player on the world-map possible. The dev has said he plans to change the upgrade system into something better and I hope he does because even though infinite upgrades is awesome, it takes forever to get there and there are no one-time upgrades that make big changes, such as an upgrade that grants a new villager type, job or building, which would make an already infinite game more replayable.

         Lastly, I still hate villager confusion - the new faith system helps, but it is still senseless to me that villagers get confused (even at max faith) when I simply pick up a few resources and move them, very irritating that they waste literal in-game hours (irl about 1 min) freaking out because I'm using powers helpfully. It doesn't make sense to me that the faithful villagers would be getting confused about the idea of their god actually helping them.

I finally managed to beat a map on survival (removing all corruption), holy hell. It truly feels like an accomplishment.

The game plays like a mix of Rimworld (for the colony management) and Kingdom (never-ending waves that get stronger and stronger until you die while you act as the hero, but in this case, a god).

You build a base, monsters raid you every night, corruption takes over the map, you try to upgrade as fast as you can and manage resources, and eventually you usually lose.

There are two ways to approach a map: the intended way, where you let the corruption slowly take over and hope to escape to the next area with as many villagers as possible while towering up with beautiful mazes, and the "I'm not losing way", where you'll read a bunch of tutorials and guides throughout the years and hope to kill the corruption before it gets out of hand. Some mobs are intended to surprise your usual construction tactics (fire elementals hate water, ghosts hate magic walls) and if you don't plan for them you're in for a rude awakening.

Both are fun and satisfying in different ways. The corruption hates when you push back against it and will send increasingly difficult waves the more you box it in. If you instead let it take over the map, you will have a generally easier time surviving, but might start becoming starved for resources to an extent. Or not, because you're a god that can regrow forests and mountains on a whim, with your amazing powers coming from sacrificial pools and Duracell battery packs/essence collectors.

The first time I played, I felt like the game was too slow and was constantly running on 3X time. This was a major mistake. Ideally, you should be doing something every second, whether it be helping to build buildings using the grab spell, or charging up mana using natural radiance pools and sacrificial pits (you can also sacrifice rocks to them!), or setting your foes on fire because your maze is very tight and you have a flame spell that actually works as a napalm spell.

As for the art direction, I like the pixel art style, but it feels like many of the buildings aren't distinct enough, as well as the spell icons. It's hard to make out what's what at a glance until you're many hours in. The music is alright but I turned it off since it feels like it could use more variety. Sometimes I have no idea what the hell colonists are doing, and I'm not sure if it's an AI issue or if it's the way I'm allocating them, but unless I specifically prioritize each job in order, it feels like nothing gets done.

Overall, really solid game, but not for everyone. Pick this one up if you like a challenge and extensive micromanagement and you miss the days of god games.

To begin with: This is a great game, especially for this low price. Getting into the mechanics of it is not that easy at first, I learned from mistakes a lot and reset my world two times, before I got a grip at it. I like the concept of building a survival RTS (much like banished) but with a growing threat that needs to be defended from.

Its biggest, yet missing, potential is in the long playability. 
There is a world map and you advance from a flourishing village to the next region on the world map. That is quite fine and gives the feel of conquering a world and prospering.
But once I have a working village, the next map is relatively easier (you can send much more villagers to a new region than you had for your first try - there could instead be just an "expedition" of fixed size that needs to be build and sent) and, secondly, I repeat the same steps on the next map - I have found the maps not to be different enough to grant a new experience. 
There could be resources scarce or even missing, needing to be imported from another village of you. 
There could be different types of monsters or disasters, needing a different response of defense. 
- e.g. a fireworld, where your wooden buildings can catch fire and need water to be rescued

I understand difficulty is mean to be a big draw of this game, I understand the whole "spend ages then die" is supposed to be intended. But there is no world where suddenly losing a twenty hour village isn't painful, and not in a good way. I've spent the last thirty in game days gradually pushing back the corruption and gauging the response from the monsters every night, keeping in mind the warning from the tutorial hint that the corruption will fight back if I deprive it of room. Everything was fine until the last few days. I was managing the monsters alright every night, they got much tougher but it was nothing my defenses couldn't deal with. Until suddenly, the corruption stops getting pushed back by fire pits. Where it would basically melt before, now it just sticks around. So what would have been the final day of corruption got dragged out into one more night, except now the monster spawns were INSANE. I killed something in the ballpark of 300-900 monsters that kept pooling out of the small collection of MAYBE one hundred tiles, and now the monsters had several thousand health instead of the low one thousand range. Defenses that were once overwhelming were immediately out scaled in the course of one night. Whatever system is used to dictate the difficulty of monsters in relation to the size of corruption needs to be tweaked.

Despite my frustration with the corruption scaling, this game is still fun. Managing my village and defenses while beating back the corruption is an engaging challenge. I'm not sure if it's a difficulty thing, but the loot crate spawns felt way too high, being able to grab something like 20 of every piece of equipment from them sorta removes the urgency for smithing related buildings.

A short while after starting a new map, corruption will start creeping in spawning enemy mobs that attack at night, which adds a bit of a tower defence element to the game. If you play smart and fast you can cut off and corner the corruption before it becomes a major threat, but this will cause it to spawn more enemies more often. If you don't want to deal with any of that the game does offer a peaceful mode with no enemies.

You also have a slew of God powers you can use, and you can grab and move around things like resources to help build and enemies to toss into death pits. It's a neat addition that adds in more direct control so you're not just sitting back watching everything happen all the time. Overall the game is pretty addictive, it's fun to see your little dudes working away and your base growing and expanding. I'm not sure how much diversity and variety in gameplay the different maps offer, as the two maps I played seemed fundamentally similar, but I've gotten like 60 hours out of it and I'm not ready to put it down yet. It is a village management game with elements of tower defense, where you have to wall off your city, and try to survive indefinitely against a corruption slowly claiming everything on the map that's not near your buildings.
You have spells to utilize as the deity of the village, using which you can ensure that your village is self-sufficient (as in, the resources that your village gathers never run out).
Honestly it feels like Rimworld Mobile. There are many things that you can't manage, micromanagement is basically non-existent (you can't choose which villagers you send to the neighbouring region to create a new village. They level up and age, so it's a weird thing to have no influence over whatsoever), art style is a minimalistic pixel-art with villagers not reflecting what they have equipped or even if they are the superior race nephilim pawns or just your average joes.
Tower defense aspect doesn't feel that good since the towers fire very slowly, and the upgrading of them goes just normal->better->even better->even better but now you can add elemental damage, there's no choice to tweak the towers in a certain direction for the most part.
You can turn villagers into rangers that can fight the monsters too, but you can improve their combat ability only by providing them with wooden swords/iron swords, armors and healing items. Notice I said 'provide', because telling them to equip better version of equipment is, again, impossible.

This game has atrocious onboarding and UI.  It loves to break conventions and does a terrible job of making it clear to players what is happening and why.

Despite this, the unique genre combo is quite enjoyable.  City builders can feel aimless, but having to tower defend provides a purpose for expansion. This is fine until you realize that enemy difficulty scales infinitely (practically).  When you know you're guaranteed to lose, the only fun is in seeing how far you can get - yet the game doesn't track records and optimizing runs is frustrating when every mechanic is opaque.  The game feels incongruous to me; I think it would be vastly improved if it picked a side between casual god game and deadly tower defense.

Ultimately, if you can accept poor UI and can handle intermittent frustration, this game has a solid amount of fun to offer.  Just don't expect the same amount of depth and replayability as many other city builders.

Rise to Ruins is a lovely city management/tower defence game that successfully blends the two genres into a very enjoyable game.

The basic premise is pretty simple; you place down building blueprints and then the pawns in your city try to build it. You then play a balancing act as you assign people to jobs freely (i.e. builder, farmer, lumberjack, etc.) in order to meet the needs of your city while also expanding, upgrading, and most importantly fortifying it.

The antagonist of the game is the Corruption which shows up after the first night and spawns monsters to attack you every night after that. The player can build an array of defensive towers and their support structures, walls and gates, as well as several different buildings that allow people to be assigned to a combat role or produce golems that protect the town.

The Corruption also expands its creep, allowing more graveyards to be built and thus more monsters to be spawned each night making it beneficial to contain it. The creep needed for graveyards to be built won't expand near your buildings so using torches, towers, or regular buildings you can build a wall where the enemies can't build (they can still come and destroy your buildings though) to limit how many they spawn. It's risky though, since the Corruption will actively try to build around this blockade if it can.

The game has a leveling system in place that rewards you periodically from milestones (like survive X days) with chests which you unlock with a currency generated by the pawns in your village doing things and building stuff. These chests reward you with powerful passive bonuses that apply permanently to your save game even if you reset the world map.

If you love rouge-likes and Dwarf Fortress, this game is up your alley, however I have some caveats and some things I love (I'll start with the caveats).

The Caveats:

1. The UI is extremely small and cloistered with no way to pause and examine things if you're eyes aren't great or to enlarge text if you need it. On top of that, when mobs are in your town it's almost impossible to select them or sometimes even see them amongst all the other things around them including the buildings that are being attacked or the resources they contain (mainly when trying to pick up and move the mob to a less destructive location). When trying to defend my town there's been times where I have to either sit back and watch the destruction because I can't intervene, hoping that it isn't too severe, or just destroy my save and start from scratch because there's no way to recover after a certain amount of setback.
2. The help text and general information surrounding what different game elements and mechanics behave is not robust. It's hard to know what choices to make for defending your territory when it comes to tower upgrades or walls. The wall help text says that it won't be attacked unless mobs have no other way around, but I've routinely had monsters destroy parts of my tower maze walls even with three tile paths perfectly open but a longer path. I love the idea of building a tower defense type pathing structure, but if the walls are vulnerable in an unpredictable way, it isn't a viable path to building.
3. Lastly, the different resistance types for monsters requires you to build a lot of different tower types despite having a fairly low building count ceiling that requires a lot other resources that require other buildings. It's hard to have the perfect mix of towers when you need a lot of support structures and citizens while also trying to build out lighting structures to keep the corruption at bay. It feels to me like threading a needle every time with very little room for improvisation or creativity in terms of what I build, when I build it, and if I built it effectively enough. I've had some games where I can already see that I'm not going to make it even though it's only 5 or 6 days in. It would be nice to have some flexibility in terms of how to get to a successful, defensible build without having to rush the initial building and resource gathering.

The Things I Love:

1. Things ain't easy. Again, like Dwarf Fortress, you get no help if you mess up, but once you learn some of the meta you can make it happen. The balance isn't perfect, such as how much the corruption ramps up when you finally manage to get it to a point where it should be eliminated, but it will put up a fight which I actually appreciate. I want a challenge and not some predictable meta where you just follow some wiki and always win.
2. Getting your essence level up feels incredible and really helps you out, but it takes the right amount of time, Sure, you're a god, and yo've got powers, but you've got to make sure that your faith level is raising or you've got nothing. It's fun trying to raise the essence storage level, and once you do it's smooth sailing for a while but it's never a breaking game mechanic. In fact, if you rely on it too much you'll ruin your chances to survive the later stages of the pressed for space corruption.
3. I'd love a few more storage spaces, or storage spaces that can hold more (or maybe a building that can create crates and barrels to help store more things) but over all I love the mix of clearly important buildings (harvesting, housing, food, defense) with minutiae (trash collecting, dog houses, rangers, lightning rods, magic stuff). It's got a great balance between stopping monsters from attacking and managing a town.
4. I like the blood moon and the trashy slime elements. It's just nice to know that no matter how much you handle the obvious enemy—the corruption—you're never safe. You're _never safe_.

Anyway, I wish the game didn't make me feel so rushed to immediately strike out space wise against the corruption and I wish I had more UI clarity so I can see what is happening and react to it. Additionally, besides the text size and information help, controlling time a bit to slow it down or speed it up would be super helpful. I think being able to drop time down to half and quarter time as well as being able to pause the game and interact with the game would be a huge win with a small amount of change.

Rating: 10/10

The Art (OMG the art is so great):
This game has the most beautiful pixel art that makes the world seem really alive. almost everywhere you see is satisfying eye candy. Almost everything in the game that isn't an inanimate object has animations. People, animals, and monsters all have unique animations for most actions, rain collectors have animated rain pooling into the funnels, rain washes off the building roofs. There are so many beautifully animated particle affects that most items or objects emit including the UI itself! Weather/environmental effects really pull you into the world what with clouds casting shadows and rain making you feel chilly in the winter/fall. Literally at any time, just zoom into your village and look at everything and you can see how much work the creator put into the art. 

The Gameplay:
When playing the game it takes your usual top-down town simulator approach and has you making resource harvesting/refining buildings and houses to feed your people and keep them out of the rain. You are essentially a god that can cast spells to do all kinds of useful actions. These spells can range from calling down lightning strikes to summoning work golems or even blessing your pregnant villagers to create demigod children with improved stats (some spells you cant do unless you have enough villagers since they increase your mana)! You start off by choosing any area on the overworld map that you want to start your empire from and then over time you can migrate villagers from that map tile to the next, slowly making a chain of kingdoms each having their own history and layout. Watch out though, you have to do all of this while trying to defend against the ever growing threat of the corruption on each map and the monster waves that spawn from there every night.

Game Mechanics:
I cant begin to tell you how many hidden and unique game mechanics this game has. The villagers all live their own lives and do their own tasks while every villager, animal and monster has their own XP bar, stats and inventory. Monsters build evil buildings in the corruption that can increase the number of spawned monsters and when you fight back the corruption (it can be done but its so hard) every tile that gets removed can spawn more monsters even during the day! For a 2d top down game you will be pleasantly surprised that the environment can be manipulated in many ways as long as you have the spellpower or the villagers with the proper jobs to do it. When playing you will find that you can build a trade center to buy and sell resources/equipment but something it doesn't outright tell you is that when you sell stuff in one village the store in another village will let you buy the stuff you just sold (quick way to move stuff from one side of the map to another). Things like this are constantly surprising me and with the new updates being added I am sure there will be more cool ideas to try to improve your gameplay.

Community content:
Unfortunately there is a severe lack of Fan content for this game so it suffers greatly when it comes to looking up specific game play mechanic tutorials or finding neat challenges to try. If the community had more content creators making gameplay mechanic tutorials or fun game play challenges I think it would be way better received by newcomers. There is some great content though so one or 2 videos will basically show you how to effectively play the game so don't despair!

Closing thoughts:
At first I suggest new players look at a couple gameplay videos to get an idea of the way of things but as you play you will definitely notice when things are and aren't working in your village as the game has many useful an intuitive stat/event tools built in game to help manage everything efficiently. I have spent countless hours managing my towns, choosing what jobs villagers should be hired to, upgrading the different resource collection systems you can make, designing/upgrading defenses and managing the waves of monsters that attack most nights. Many, many nights I've realized it was way late and had to go to bed or I wouldn't get enough sleep because I am always needing to prepare for the next nights defence or fix an issue that popped up due to overpopulation or some random event. I will continue to play this game for a very long time and I suggest anyone who is curious and likes pixel art or town simulator games to give it a try!

I love Rise to Ruins. It's a game I keep coming back to from time to time and play a bunch of hours of, then let it lie and have the dev work on some updates, then play it like it's a whole new game all over again. Every time a new update comes out, it's an additional layer of polish and love that the dev has dedicated to the game, and it shows. It's been really fun following the game mature more and more into what I imagine its final state to be; and every time the dev surprises me in pleasant ways as to which direction we're going in with this.

This mixes my favourite three genres together in a beautifully unique itch of God Game, RTS and Colony Sim, with some Tower Defence elements sprinkled in for good measure. It's got great humour, the music is fantastic, and the graphics have this unique and hand-crafted feel to them. Level design is unique, and there's a lot of maps! Plus, you get to design your own with the Map Editor (I can feel my pre-teen self from way back yonder cry out in joy). Finally, it has this Roguelite-esque / Idle Game progression system that I really enjoy, with some tongue-and-cheek references to loot box mechanics without falling victim to the predatory nature of those as often seen in AAA games.

Where the game is missing some polish is primarily in the UX department. The Level Editor primarily has some woes; eg. you can't erase a tile underneath a building without also getting rid of that building, and to switch from placing tiles to placing buildings, you have to completely switch contexts, which takes multiple clicks. This is the same in the base game too, where to switch between roads and buildings you have to perform the same action. Furthermore, the game doesn't remember your UI settings from playthrough to playthrough, so every time you start a new game, you have to do some initial setup, which could be streamlined. As far as criticism goes, I feel that's a rather minor (and personal) set of gripes. I've found in the past that using VoiceAttack to automate some of the frequent clicking / mouse movements away is a nice band-aid for me.

I have never in any playthrough experienced noticeably buggy behaviour, which makes this a unique game among all games I've ever played. Even the most polished and cared-for games I know, I can point out some exploit or bug. The only things I've noticed is one or two crashes in 372 hours of playtime (yeah really), and that the AI that drives the townspeople does things I can't necessarily predict. Eg. if I assign a new lumberjack task, it's not necessarily the lumberjack that's closest by who will pick up that job. But the behaviour *is* consistent; learning how to interact with the AI and work around its particular quirks is one of the learning curves of RtR for sure, but once you get good at that, you hardly notice it anymore.

On occasion, I've found myself a little bored waiting for things to happen. But I've come to learn over time, that this only ever happens when you've actually set something up inefficiently and/or made a mistake in your design. Every time you start a new map or use the Doom World option to reset all the maps (saving your unlockables!), you tackle the game slightly differently, slightly better, a little bit more interestingly. It's fun to experiment in this game, and there are many strategies that can work perfectly fine for you. My most recent playthrough involves very little base defences, no monster maze, a couple of golem spawners, and five Cullis Gates to drop monsters into if they overwhelm the defences.

I can only recommend Rise to Ruins. I've had nothing but fun with it for a really good amount of time. Well worth your money.

Rise to Ruins is one of those games that really hits the sweet spot if you're into god sims or city-builders with a twist. It’s like it knows exactly what itch to scratch, blending the satisfaction of managing a village with the chaos of survival.

As a god in the game, you’re not just watching your villagers build huts and gather resources—you’re actively involved. You can heal them, control the weather, and even throw down some godly wrath if things get out of hand. It feels like you're guiding them but also constantly reacting to the world. And that balance between control and unpredictability is what makes it so engaging.

What I love most is how everything just clicks. You’re building this peaceful little village, but at the same time, there’s this looming threat from monsters that come at night. So while you're expanding and gathering resources during the day, you’re also preparing to defend everything you’ve built. It adds just the right amount of tension.

And honestly, the game has this really addictive loop. You’re constantly improving things, tweaking your strategy, and watching your village grow from a few huts to a thriving settlement. Plus, the retro pixel art style just gives it that extra charm.

If you’re looking for a game that scratches that god-sim itch while keeping things fresh with a mix of management and survival, Rise to Ruins is a must-try. It’s challenging but in a way that feels rewarding, and you’ll get sucked in for hours without even realizing it.

Things that should be fixed or adapted in my opinion (This is after 150+hrs, so some of them might just be an issue with my playstyle):


* Trash at this point is little more than an annoyance which doesn't really contribute anything to the game apart from adding another aspect that needs to be managed. You can make walls with trashy cubes, but that's about all you can do with it while you are forced to waste around 4 building slots on it early on already. Along with this, everything made with trash lowers the appeal of the area it's built on, so all this system does is force the player to deal with trash for no other reason than dealing with trash.


* Food production is slow as hell, i've tried pretty much every set-up suggested on steam forums and on other pages i could find, have it close to a lake, have a purifier next to it, have a bottler, however nothing seems to work for me (if i'm doing anything wrong please let me know). Also, Farms are supposed to be self-sufficient, currently the farmers take food from the map > plant it in farm > harvest > go back to taking food from the map. 
While it should be, Take food from map > plant seeds in farm > harvest > take seeds from harvest > replant in farm > repeat. There is no reason why they have to farm from the map once again once they have a farm up and running.

Same goes for meat collection in clucker coops and animal pens, the rate at which animals get brought in and the rate at which meat is produced is a fraction of what is needed, this is especially the case when you play on custom and play around with the nomads spawnrate.


* The learning curve is steep, but in the wrong places. This game has a lot of features that aren't new, therefore everyone with a bit of experience in comparable games wouldn't take too long familiarizing themselves with the options, interface and gameplay. The steep learning curve that's mentioned applies to certain gameplay mechanics that do not get mentioned in the tips, so even if you follow the tips to the letter you will still have to google for most parts that will actually confuse you.

If you up the amounts of lumberjacks and miners you will see a large increase in work speed, the same goes for builders. As an avid fan of Act Raiser from my childhood days of yore on the SNES, this game is it's true spiritual successor and does what the devs could only dream to have done. It has many similarities to popular titles such as Dwarf Fortress, but does not suffer many of the same flaws. In DF, for example, you have highly specialized dwarves that feel terrible to individually lose if you want to play the game with combat on. Exploit the game with danger rooms and trap corridors, or don't bother dealing with combat. Corrupted biomes? Flat out forget it lest you deal with flying buffalo fur terrifying your dwarves into starvation.

Rise to Ruins gets the combat angle right. The game on Nightmare difficulty is highly punishing, and dooming words is a regular occurence (60 some hours of play in, and I still haven't got through my first winter.) However, successfully navigating it feels extremely good and the challenge is not as static as the tower defense angle shown in the trailer. Carving out map control is essential for being able to manage the tougher seasons like Winter, but the game doesn't let you do it for free. Settling up mazes is a novelty -- you'll have things flying over your walls, elementals blasting down your front door, and blood moons raining fire and mayhem into your town proper.

The end result is a fantastic world simulator with very unique maps, some which seem nice to embark on initially and others where it feels like you need to succeed on an easy map and feed the harder map to even stand a chance. God powers and cullis gates at first feel overpowered, but as you make it later in the game you realize it's all extremely well balanced and everything comes with a cost.. Balancing all the different environmental needs and roguelite elements of the city management along with the intensity of the encroaching corruption is extremely difficult to manage but very rewarding to conquer. Not once have I felt like any of my failed settlements were a result of anything other than me needing to play better.

Simply put, if you want Dwarf Fortress smashed together with Act Raiser and the potential for a very challenging world building simulator, this game's for you. The Dev is a one man team who clearly cares immensely about the game and has a solid head on his shoulders for gameplay, aesthetic, and balance. Don't pass this one up if you're a fan of the genre.

Villager AI is sometimes incredibly stupid, and what constitutes a dangerous environment or an undesirable time to actually do some work for once is either really inconsistent or really vague. If lumberjacks won't clear trees near a fire elemental, repairmen shouldn't repair the slightly damaged fire pit next to him. And if the bowyer is swimming in silk, I expect full cylinders firing on quiver production, instead of the French-style "we'll get to it when we feel like it" mentality that most refined and manufacturing villagers tend to hold. Very tempting to soak one or two of those slackers in Cullis Gate goo to set an example...
The big reason I write this review is to help spread the word of the great middle ground that most reviewers seem to either miss or ignore. Yes, the game starts as a town builder and transitions into a steadily tougher tower defense game. But each town map can be completely cleared of corruption, turning the tower defense into a once in a Blood Moon insurance policy, and turning that town into a economic powerhouse for all surrounding maps. 
To explain: World map is broken up into lots of strategic maps. Each scenario has a single spawn point for the enemy, that grows over time. But your buildings prevent the spread of the corruption. And one building, fire pits, both have great anti-corruption properties and are totally ignored by enemies. To boot, if any building is built near corruption, over time, it will force the tainted land to return to its former self, preventing enemy spawns. Repeat this cycle until all the corrupted land is removed, and it will never return on that scenario. Ever.
Fire pits remove corrupted land, but enemy buildings also have to go. Thankfully, the game also has automated golems to help your towers defend. But these golems consider ANY build space your town, including around fire pits. Build a pit near an enemy structure, and your golems will swarm on the attack and obliterate it, keeping your fragile villagers safe.

Hopefully this long winded guide-within-a-review helps both old and new players understand that the objective of the game is pacification, not resistance, and the game is a really great hybrid of a lot of genres. Use the advantage of infinite golems and glory to your nascent empires!

Rise to Ruins is a prime example of what happens when you mix a mad scientist, a sadist, a succubus, and an indie developer into a a single, perverse being. They sit and think about all of the ways they can grind you through their torture machine for their own amusement, and make you want to come back for more again and again.

Rise to Ruins effectively merges Tower Defense-like, RTS-like, and Colony Builder-like into a beautiful tapestry of pixelated wonder. The attention to detail signifies the game as a labor of life by a gamer that understands gaming. Distinct effort was placed into ensuring the typical trappings of the parent genres didn't plague the experience as you lead your colony against the horrors of the Corruption.

Of the big three, it hits all in spades:

-- Replayability -- *****
-- Immersion -- *****
-- Accessibility -- *****

Replayability = "How much would you enjoy coming back to this game for another round after spending several cycles making progress" 

Because of the difficulty curve (and the learning curve, to a lesser extent), Rise to Ruins provides more than enough challenge to keep you engaged as you play, and keep you thinking about effective strategies during down-time. Not only does each zone present its own challenge and strategy, you cannot progress in the game until you have conquered *at least* one zone - a tall order for the newly initiated (hint: Try Applemeadow).

Immersion = "How easy is it to forget the passing of time and devote all of your sensory bandwidth to the gaming experience?"

Every game  and genre handles this differently but one aspect of immersion is universal; the soundtrack. Rise to Ruins absolutely kills it in the audio department by effectively delivering a tranquil and meditative soundtrack, and a dynamic array of SFX to get you engaged with the goings on in the world. Visually, the pixelated art on your many denizens is efficient and just detailed enough for you to tell the difference between the various job roles, species, and unit types.

Accessibility = "How tough is it to figure out what's going on and understand the 'rules of the game' without looking at external resources (i.e. content NOT created by the developer/developer-funded resources)"

Because of the clear interface and RIDICULOUS number of tool-tips (a good thing), Rise to Ruins isn't difficult to learn. The hardest aspect (for the uninitiated) is the need to accept that you will lose, a lot. And often for stupid (and easily avoidable) reasons. Unfortunately, that doesn't bring back the 3 hours you spent on your prospering settlement. Look at each play-through as a 'Run', and appreciate the high level of replayability the game offers. 

One thing Rise to Ruins has that no other game has is Tiberiumkyle. If you have a question about Rise to Ruin, *any* question, Tiberiumkyle (Community Manager Extraordinare) has your back. In fact, there are many helpful voices in the Rise to Ruin discord, a testiment to how rabid the fanbase is for this amazing game.

TL;DR

Buy if you wished tower defense games had more substance and colony-builder content in them
Buy if you're looking for a challenging title that can provide a relaxing and meditative distraction during your downtime
Buy if you're you're interested in high-replayability, colony builders, and/or games that can be frustratingly difficult for totally bullshit [and legitimate... face it, you weren't paying attention when the enemy attack came, were you?] reasons

This was my old review. I have had a change of heart with this game. It has a rather steep learning curve. Mainly due to how the game now plays. This review now talks about a lot of solutions I have solved and a lot of ways I have made the game more 'efficient'. 






At the time I had not understood how to optimize my gameplay. For example, I was being very inefficient using the Trash Burners instead of using the Cullis Gate... A landfill + cullis gate = more efficiency than ever before, infinite energy, and constant production even during high influx of combat and towers needing loads of energy. 

Always build High-Quality buildings for maximum Faith and to make villagers sleep faster so they can go to work sooner. 

Magic damage > Arrows, Stone Ammo -  It's simply a no brainer. Many enemies do resist magic, but a large majority of them suffer from a lack of magic resistance. Combine this with your golems for immense power. 

Spam Crystal Golems and Stone Golems. Wood golems are useless in combat and are immense resource hogs since wood often times has more risk of being destroyed / consumed more than stone due to the terrain health they have being lower than stone (obv it's wood...!)

Always use holy trees to build "True" Walls. What I mean by this, is that any kind of terrain on the map, ANY, kind of terrain, let that be a single 'dead' tree that can block AI pathing, it WILL block AI pathing, meaning that you can easily snake paths through the world and seperate the corruption slowly overtime. 

DO NOT BUILD BALLISTAS FOR OFFENSIVE USE. I have had so many times where I thought " This would be the perfect siege tool! " Only for it to backfire as I spawn 8 zombies, 4 slimes, 6 skeletons and 3 fire elementals, who are all lvl 30+ (or at times even 40+) who immediately destroy stuff I was not prepared to defend. 

Water is both your friend, and enemy. Do not be afraid to build a moat around, or inside of your walls, even, as Fire Elementals treat water like any other terrain and will avoid it at any cost unless there is no other way to go. In which they will find the weakest point in your defenses and destroy your base from behind your back. I remember spending a whole day trying to keep them away from my home not realizing that a comet I had spawned in front of my main gate accidentally cut off their only 'true' path into the city, causing them to go and destroy tree and rock terrain to get into my city and essentially flood it with flames. 

Do not build paths until you actually have dirt paths carved from natural movement your villagers and golems make. Then you can build paths on the most efficient route they take. ( Or plan ahead meticulously if you'd like lol)

ALWAYS use rain whenever you can to deter Fire Elementals, as they take massive damage from rain and treats it as if they are actually inside of water taking damage overtime. Which, I am not 100% sure, I believe it stacks on top of normal water as well. 

Food and Water is never an issue. Build WELLS and FARMS right next to eachother, and then a single bottler. The wells produce more water than a water purifier if you place 4 (or 9) of them together in a 2x2 (3x3) square. The bottlers will fill the High Quality buildings, Camp, Storage of any kind, Villager inventories, etc. And over-produce water for your village to use and drink from. 

Always. Make. Tools. Production is sped up by like 4x or 6x the normal speed without tools. Stockpile on that iron or buy a ton of stuff with the gold you get!

Don't be afraid to sell souls. That's a LOT of cash for a lot of nothing! A single villager is negligible later on. 

Always have max Occulists, or as much as possible, for incredible Essence and Faith generation. This is a must have for any village if you do not have this then say goodbye in the second season. Always put them as close as possible to your High Quality buildings for as much essence generation as possible.

I cannot think of anything else to put here. But there are so many cheaper ways to keep your village alive that does not need traditional means or the 'typical' survival choices of buildings. 

Live long, prosper, and Rise to Ruins!

Rise to Ruins has been a delightful surprise in the Early Access scene, offering a refreshing mix of strategy and survival elements. From the moment I started building my first village, I was hooked by the game's ability to balance resource management with the thrill of tower defense.

The game presents a world where corruption spreads, and monsters threaten your villagers, adding a layer of tension to the otherwise peaceful task of building and expanding. The attention to detail in the pixel artstyle is commendable, and the music sets a perfect tone for the atmosphere of the game.

One of the standout features is the villagers themselves, who have distinct needs and behaviors, making the management aspect deeply engaging. The introduction of a lifespan for villagers adds a new layer of strategy, as you must balance their immediate needs with the long-term health of your community.

The tower defense component is challenging and rewarding, with the game cleverly ramping up the difficulty as you progress. The ability to share resources and villagers between multiple villages on the overworld map is a welcome addition that adds to the game's complexity and depth.

While the game is still in Early Access, the developer has shown a commitment to updating and improving the game, which is promising for its future. Rise to Ruins is a gem that offers a lot of bang for your buck, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for a game that combines strategy, management, and a touch of retro charm.

This is a very good game.  Like people say its a god game with tower defense and colony building.  I've seen people say that its slow paced, but your not playing the game right if that is the case IMO.  In the beginning it is slower because you have less colonists and all resources are individual units and all have to be harvested, refined, bought, etc.  Colonists depending on their level will carry a stack of resources to the build site, drop them off and build piece by piece.  This is done very well and makes resources have more meaning than just numbers, more tangible.  With god powers however you can speed things up.  With the hand tool you can pick up resources and drop them on a building project and it adds to them.  When your not doing that you've most likely run out of magic so you should be collecting that and repeating.  If you need resources you can mass harvest or use the hand to pick them up one at a time.  Barring all that head on up to the corruption and pick up some of the enemy builders that step into open and drop them in the cauldron or in front of your towers.  Burn down their buildings, drop meteors, earthquakes and really just be a straight up bully to that poor corruption.  If you want you can try to bless a female villager and birth a nephalim.  The more villagers you get the more magic capacity, so it takes a bit to become a true god.

Long story short, you really should not be idling unless you want to.  Also there are speed controls so, you know.... use them.  For 15 bucks this game is well worth that plus dev is still adding stuff, albeit slowly, but game is complete now so everything from here on is a bonus.

[h1]Core Mechanics[/h1]
This is where this game really shines. I've always been a lover of the City Builder and Tower Defense genres, so finding a game like this that belongs to both genres has always been a dream for me. I found it, and it lived up to the expectations. If you like both genres, you will like this game. In Rise to Ruins you must try to expand your village and also defend it, and all that without direct control over your population, because you play as a God entity.

As an oldschool Warcraft 3 TD player, something I really love about this game is the ability to maze things, to be able to direct monsters in the most bizarre and creative ways. I always preferred this sort of TD over the ones with fixed positions for towers.

The City Builder segment is also complex, you will discover very quickly that you must think about the logistics in your village expansion. Doing everything disorderly may be your doom. There are many Data & Statistics views/information avaiable to help you make your decisions.

And there's also the God Game part of the game. As the God entity of your civilization, you have access to many spells, so you can help them survive the dangers of the world. The spells are important in the survival of your worshippers and feel correctly balanced.

The game also has features like Weather and Seasons, so you need to adapt to your current situation.

There are also perks, that function similarily to roguelikes. As you progress in the game, you will receive perks that are permanent even if you decide to doom (reset) your world, in case you feel like everything really fell apart and you want a clean restart. So that's a good rewarding way of making failing less frustrating.

[h1]Story, Lore and Character Depth[/h1]
None. There is no story/campaign. It's pure sandbox. I personally prefer games with story/campaign but I didn't mind the lack of it in this game, it still got me hooked. Perhaps it was even for the best, to allow you to imagine your own village story and your own goals.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
It's a very well done pixelated style, it fits the game atmosphere and mixed genre perfectly.

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
I usually don't include soundtrack on my reviews, even though I really appreciate a good one. But I found this one to be quite beautiful and worth mentioning.

[h1]Bugs[/h1]
Eventually something may become weird in your world or in your people's AI, but you can easily reset everyone's AI or rollback to a previous save. I haven't encountered a single gamebreaking bug. But in case you do, the developer is extremely responsive.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Ultimately, I loved this game. I honestly didn't image I would play this game for so long. If you like City Builder & Tower Defense & God game genres or even like the idea of these genres combined, it's an easy buy, Rise to Ruins is very well done. You won't regret it.
