Rise to Ruins is a fun mix of tower defence, god game, and village/colony sim. The basic premise is you are a God overseeing your villagers and helping them survive against the ever encroaching threat of the corruption. 

The corruption is the main antagonist, it slowly consumes everything that your influence doesn't reach and sends waves of monsters to destroy your villagers every night. It can't be beaten, it can only be contained and the more constrained it feels, the harder it fights back. (well it can be beaten, but it requires extensive knowledge of the game or cheese that defeats the whole point of playing on anything but peaceful mode)

The main gameplay loop is fun and will eat up more of your time than you expect. You build your village, establish industries to support it and develop defences to protect it. The learning curve can seem steep at times and you will most likely fail many times over before you've gotten a solid grasp on the mechanics, but it is a fun and rewarding experience. 

There is a roguelite progression system that helps with the learning curve and keeps things from getting stale to quickly. You are rewarded xp after every session, success or failure. You can use this xp to open perk chests that give you ever increasing bonuses to almost every aspect of the game. Sometimes you may open one and think "Cool down reduction on a spell I don't use, meh". Other times you will get something that makes you rethink your entire approach in order to make use of it. You also aren't locked to your first region, you can send migrants and supplies to neighbouring regions which you can use to establish a new village and there is enough variety in the different maps to keep it from feeling "samey". Plus, you can always return to an older region/village at anytime without losing progress anywhere else (which can allow for some interesting interaction between your settlements)

The difficulty is fully configurable and you can alter pretty much any part of the game's difficulty/mechanics to suit your tastes or create unique challenges (Extreme length winters present more challenges than you would think).

The biggest complaint I have is that there isn't a ton of depth or variety, once you've found a strategy that works you won't find yourself forced to change your approach very much, and something that you've safely ignored will most likely stay ignored unless you want to challenge yourself/mix things up. 

The Dev is still very active, and actually just released a large content update that added several new things (including achievements) and changed the way the faith/influence system works as well. It was a great update that has resulted in me putting another 60+ hours into the game.

Overall, even though Rise to Ruins may lack the depth of the various games/genres that inspired it, it blends those different genres successfully to create a unique and fun experience. Seriously, just look at my hours played; that is an absolutely absurd amount of value for the ~$20 CAD I paid for it.

This is a colony building-roguelike-tower defense-god simulator mashup. A really interesting combination of genres.
The premise is that you start on a map, build out your colony and survive the onslaught of the "corruption". You then migrate to a new map and do the same all over again. 

The graphics have so much pixely goodness that you just cannot fault it. The music is fantastic and matches the game perfectly and the game loop is extremely addictive. 

Some (maybe) important things to take note of:

1) The game is brutal on the higher difficulty levels so take care if you venture there.

2) The game is not really "winnable". The whole premise of the game is to survive the onslaught of corruption and by doing better and pushing the corruption further, you only get more and more resistance from the enemy. This is one of the main problems I have with the game as it seems kind of unfair as the better you do, you get more and more punished for it. Having that said, "beating" a map by removing all corruption is possible but an extremely hard thing to do.

3) The game can feel that you are doing the same thing over and over again which in a sense is true. Even though each map is unique and poses different challenges, you build out your colony, survive and move on. Once you have a working recipe for survival you execute it and that's it. On higher difficulty levels, if you F up something, things start cascading usually and you get overrun.

4) There is no win condition. This is mostly a sandbox game even though it does not seem like one, and you make your own goals and wins as you please.

Performing actions in that region accrues god points, which you spend on randomized perks that apply to ALL regions. Even if you fail and have to doom your town because you goofed your build order (a common occurrence), you're still making gradual, tangible progress. Your villagers get a little strong, your towers hit a little harder, you build houses a little faster, and so on.

Big fan of the art style as well. The pixel art on the structures is wonderfully detailed, and all the chirps and grunts of the villagers reminds me of Settlers 2, one of my favorite games of all time.

A hidden gem. Shame the developer is a bit of a conservative crank on Twitter and incapable of keeping his promise of regular updates. It's fully-featured as-is, at least.

It's been a little while since I last dived into this one, but it's a great game that has unfortunately gotten some bad reviews recently due to the two developers having a lot going on and not being able to put as much time into the project as they would like. They've recently jumped back into active development on the game, though, and what they've recently added and are planning on adding in the near future sounds great. In fact, the reason I hadn't returned to the game was because I knew achievements were coming, and now they're here.

This game is a lot of fun. It's a mix of a solid and fleshed out city builder combined with challenging tower defense style gameplay. The player picks a starting location on both the world and local maps, then has to balance working on developing a small village while fighting off a growing horde of monsters born from a corruption that is spreading across the land. The corruption usually starts far from the player, but spreads inexorably toward the village. Walls can keep the corruption at bay, but as soon as it can no longer spread, the corruption becomes relentlessly aggressive, sending huge and powerful armies to break down the walls and overrun the village. Once a village becomes large enough, the player can send migrants to another area of the world map, bringing valuable supplies to a new area that may be safer from the corruption... for now.

Even when they aren't fighting hordes of monsters, the villagers' lives, and the player's time, are never dull. There are many buildings to construct such as farms to ensure that the villagers have food to eat, forges to ensure that your village has robust defenses, towers that can fire on monsters from a distance, clinics to keep your villagers in good health, and many more. Rather than giving orders to villagers directly, the player designates tasks (such as harvesting materials) and the villagers will automatically choose and perform those tasks. If the player does want (or, in rare instance, need) to micromanage, the player can reassign jobs, change their priority, and otherwise make sure things are running smoothly.

A lot of times when games try to mix two (or more) genres, the elements of each different genre individually feel lacking or overly simplified compared to games that focus on only one genre. Rise to Ruins' village building gameplay is fleshed out and complex while the tower defense style combat is challenging and gives many options for the player to survive (or not) the relentless waves of monsters. Whenever my villages have inevitably succumbed to the onslaught, rather than growing despondent, I always find myself with ideas on what might have gone wrong and what I can do next time to make it right.

If you're a fan of city builders and tower defense style games, this may be the best blend of the two genres that exists. And though development was slow for a long time, the team is back and working to make the game even better.

It's very cryptic. There's no actual tutorial. As many have said here, villagers keep dying from starvation, and you, the player are left to wonder what's even happening. I've now sunk almost a 100 hours into the game and I still don't understand the food mechanics completely.

Here's a more in depth example of maybe the biggest downfall of the game:

There is a *complete lack of proper notifications* and the visuals are hard to understand.

There's no notification, for example, for when an enemy is within your village, attacking your villagers, or even destroying your buildings. Then you suddenly get notified that 5 villagers died almost in an instant, and your screen shakes as a few buildings collapse, due to them having been taking damage from an enemy mob for the last minute or so, which you didn't know was happening. You can't for example distinguish the screen shake effect of a meteor hit, which are very common, and a building collapsing. Ok, well now you at least know the enemy is within your village, right? Good thing you have a grab tool and banish spell that you can use to move unwanted enemies elsewhere, right? Well, that would be the case, if you could distinguish what's even happening on your screen. There's like 40 villagers and 30 animals running in every direction with exclamation points or question marks above their heads. Then there's the massive amount of clutter caused by the destroyed buildings, then there's the magic effects, with pixelated fire and purple fizzing, and finally there are the enemies in your base, who either blend in with the panicking villagers, or they hiding behind villager sprites who are attacking the enemies, or then they might hide within the buildings they are attacking. All you would have to do is cast spells at or grab these enemies and your problem would be solved. You might have already fixed what was causing the enemies getting inside your village. Too bad it's nearly impossible to get rid of the enemies inside the village, as you will be completely unable to distinguish anything from this mess. Try to grab that pesky skeleton or zombie child? Nah, here's a random animal or a piece of trash for you. Managed to grab a fire elemental that killed +5 villagers? Well, plenty more will die and buildings will collapse, as you can't distinguish which villagers or buildings the elemental set on fire.

For some reason I'm still a little drawn to this game, I really would have wanted to enjoy it. The idea is great, I think, but the execution has a lot of room for improvement. It's just far too messy, cryptic, and in general, it's not a game that's pleasant to look at. All in all, it just feels tedious to play. I do not recommend buying it, unless it's on sale and less than 5 euros. If you do buy it, get ready to be very frustrated.

Game lacks basic QoL the genre invented decades ago.  Namely:

Click to drag the map.  No, too easy.  Instead, you right click to steer the map (in the opposite direction of dragging) in a floaty manner.

Pausing while navigating menus.  You can pause the game at any time.  But you can't pause while mousing over tooltips, placing buildings, or allocating jobs.  This isn't a necessary feature in your average competitive RTS (starcraft for example), but in a complicated PvE game - especially with a doom timer (They Are Billions, Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress) - the ability to pause and issue commands while paused is necessity for the average gamer.  

After encoutnering the above, I checked to see if I was missing something.  I wasn't.  The above issues aren't isolated incidents. Gameplay loops too complicated for the AI and pathfinding to solve, depressing gameplay loop where losing is inevitable, special abilities that quickly become micro intensive or outright useless, so on and so forth.  Moral of the story:  NEVER buy a game based off the positive reviews.  Check the negative reviews first!

I don't thumbs down because the game is not good. Once you figure out you're pretty much pidgeon-holed into a primarily tower defense game that eventually ends in a loss it's too late. Even if the eventual goal is too ultimately lose, there's no illusion of hope or progress. Simply put, there is ABSOLUTE ZERO offensive options for the player to use to beat back corruption inside the realm of what the developer ulitately designed the game for. To be fair, you can use the rules of the game to push your pixelites into corrupted territory to fight but it is very clear in practice this is not what the developer intended and as far as I can tell, he has no intention of implementing such a mechanic. I still think the game would be perfect for fans of peaceful townbuilding games that felt something like banished needed a more omnipresent threat than just the seasons and I think that the influences of games like simcity, rimworld, dwarf fortress, and other titles shine through brilliantly- especially with the use of god powers like black & white.
It is an absolutely killer townbuilder/tower defense game but the old school RTS gameplay advertised in my opinion only stretches as far as the GUI and overall aesthetic of the game. Offensive options just plain need to be there in some way to realize that specific ambition further. At the end of the day though, this game has no reason not to sell to its target audience and i believe that the developer has every right to make the game that he wants so thumbs down aside, great job man.

I don't think the game is close to finished at all. I don't like playing it and most of the mechanics in the game are unsatisfying rather than to the contrary. I played a dozen games in this genre, and this is the most unsatisfying one by far. Maybe I'm an outlier, but this game is not fun if you want to play optimally. The mechanics are nice, but over all the game works against you. The production industries are nice, and road and wall building is great for building fortresses, but there is an overall lack of enjoyment having to deal with the subpar, space inefficient user interface and clickfest mechanics.

+ The game has unique graphics, music, and art direction.
- The event sounds are painful and useless If it is raining -> I can't hear anything. If there are any jobs going on in the screen region, I can't hear anything. You can't fine tune the individual sounds. I want to hear monsters in my base instead of random ambient noise.
- I have a tough time distinguishing units from my base and the enemy. The pixel graphics are low resolution for individual guys, and there is a lot of eye candy distractions.
+ The game has a unique grand campaign (conquer an island).
- The game has zero story. Yes, nil. Nada.  (this is fine for me, but it's a shame, really as there is a lot of missed potential. The corruption mechanic is a great antagonist and even a cookie cutter story would have been appreciated). Take for instance Creeper World 3: Arc Eternal. That's a game with a plain story, but it works.
+ Building mechanics like a typical village simulator (villagers need minimal micro management, just macro)
- The "essence" on the map is cool on first, but then gets annoying after a while, since its hyperactive in visuals for no reason. Like a sparkly locust you want to disable.
- The chest mechanic is also cool at first (point and click to find and gather), but it often involves 300 clicks for an odd non-flowing reason. Nothing in the game involves this much clicks, and the path finding on the chest is annoying when it goes away from your village and the jump range is too short.
- The influence mechanic is fun, but there's only 3 select powers I ever need. The rest are either eye candy or actually quite useless. For instance, the resurrect dead is nice, but I can never find my dead, the '?" box that pops up often doesn't have ghosts near it.
- The user interface is hardly polished and hides most actions and information behind many clicks for no reason. Consider the left side panel for job allocation. I can cut 75% the screen real estate (empty space, running workers, redundant information) and show more jobs. But nope, I got to scroll often 2-3 times to find the job I want to increase *every* time. Things like this turn me off from the game, because its not like we're working with dwarf fortress where you can just learn the shortcuts and feel good you are learning 1337 skills, no, it feels like I'm in the 00's and I'm filling in a web form for a widget factory. You have to wrestle with your mouse the user interface every time. If you don't want to, you are forced to play sub-optimally because of these pain points ( hot swapping jobs for efficiency) can be avoided.
- The storage mechanism is painful. For instance I had trouble locating suspicious keys on the UI tallies, despite buying them on the market place. I spent 30 minutes going close to full organizer job allocation to see if it just needed to be hauled, but alas, I gave up. No loot boxes for me I guess. Ditto for any other material. This is one of the times I recall and appreciate how dwarf fortress properly had a ledger for material-to-map-position. The "Grab" ability would have been much more useful with it.
- The trash mechanic is nice, but if you have any *one* large building destroyed by enemies, *many* trash tiles are created. Trash fills up fast too, but once I played one game with this mechanic it was manageable.
- Game crashed with a null pointer error once. Yes I have autosaves. I don't know if the developer got a crash log... I only expect NPE from moddable games (like Star Sector or such) where its low development budget. I got a NPE the first hour doing nothing surprising.
- The win mechanic is unrealistic. Survive one year in every region? There's at least twenty regions... Perhaps the developers have a higher play time than most players, because after one region I've seen most of the mechanics and want to play dwarf fortress instead.
+ The world map chest mechanic is nice, but is in-your-face grindy and I'm opting to not play, because...

After building a few of everything and exploring what i believe to be every avenue of the game in under 6 hours i found myself very confused by the games popularity. It is the most basic management game I've seen that does virtually nothing to set itself apart from others like it. The two main differences are golems and corruption. You get three flavors of golems, move along. Corruption is tainted land you can do painfully little about because unless you build up the ENTIRE map it doesn't stop spawning things. With those out of the way here's a list of things the game does worse than its' competition.

Your villagers are worse than the stereotypical medieval bumpkin they emulate. They will build a wall to block a chokepoint off, procede to WALK THROUGH the wall they just built, then stand on that side of the wall until they starve to death because pathfinding must not work outside of my build zone. Is the AI meant to do this?

Speaking of the build zone, it is the absolute most infuriating thing in the game. You know how certain games require you to build power lines to connect your buildings? Instead of needing to construct additional pylons because machines need power you have to build a fire every 10 squares. This is a medieval survival game therefore your citizens don't feel safe making a building without being able to feel the warmth of a fire. I say feel the warmth because for whatever reason if you build anything next to a fire it completely blocks off the build zone. Have fun daisy chaining a dozen fires down to the next bottleneck in the terrain, it'l take two days in game to dismantle everything if you didn't put a small fire in the middle of your defensive wall. It feels so gimmicky like it was just thrown there because it seemed like a clever mechanic.

Did you know each of your citizens have an intelligence score? Wow, maybe it's like Rimworld and the smart guys get to be wizards or something! No. They don't. There aren't any non laborer jobs besides being a guard. It's even easier to get them the best armor in the game because you need 3 buildings to do so which are all available from the start. Your citizens are doing the same tasks as the 10+ people next to them for the rest of the game with the only difference being leveling up.

Your free upkeep defensive options are the guards and your basic towers. In order to survive after your first blood moon you need golems and magic towers both of which cost fairy dust. This means the only thing you need to concentrate on after the early game is fairy dust. Que 3 sets of gatherers, refiners, golem makers and watch them slap everyone into your late game. There is no other way to do this, it is a rigid system that requires fairy dust. Even your best guards will die and because you gain people equivilant to a person per day you cannot hope to keep up with the hordes of enemies with any casualty rate. This is not a complaint that you need to do certain things in order to win. This is a complaint that no matter where you set up your village and no matter what the terrain is like and no matter how many times you play it will be the same exact thing over and over. No different units. No different towers. No different maze walls. After your first blood moon its pump fairy dust into metal golems and ballista towers until your bored. There is a clear optimized build that cannot be changed and that means your replayability extends to your second village when you know the controls.

Oh wait theres that god mode element right? Shooting fireballs and bringing back people from the dead? Don't do it. The only thing I used my benevolent powers for was growing crops and spawning holy golems during the blood moon. But in all honesty this feature can be safely and completely ingnored in a successful game. Especially once you realize you can't break the stupid corrupted graveyards with a meteor because.... I don't know. Maybe the corrupted land forms some kind of shield generator into space. In which case I should build on it because my village gets plastered with earthquakes and flaming meteors twice a season while the enemies remain unscathed! It would make sense that as god i smite the enemies of my people right? Or maybe protect them from some calamity like an earthquake? Can i part the river or something? Nope you can use 2 flaming rocks on your own village to help defend against the 20 enemies raiding them. No thanks, I'll stick to making carrots grow, I don't think i'll make much of a difference anyway.

This review is already frightening in length, though much of it could have been overlooked had i not seen the game was released 4 years ago. What in the actual hell is in this game that requires 4 years? Braid took a year to make then the rest of the time was spent on artwork. If anyone reading this has attended a college class or short seminar for game development then you know the first thing they tell you is how hard it is to make it in the industry. The second is that if you want any hope of making a living off your game you have to make it something unique and put some of your own blood into its' creation. There is potential here, but given the time that has already gone into development and how much the game still looks like a horizontal slice I cannot recommend it.

The game does a terrible job actually teaching you how to play; I went the entire first day without resources because it was never brought to my attention that I actually had to assign trees and stone to be cut, or if the tooltip had popped up telling me so, it was one of the ones that suddenly vanished from view before I got the chance to click on it.

And I figured, fine, I'll delete this save and give it another go.

You cannot delete a save. Once a village is created you can't delete it, or if you can, it again does a poor job communicating how to.

So I followed through, and got decimated because of the frankly punishing building limits. In order to even get food and water that your townspeople need you need to take up several building slots, and in order to have homes you need to take up more building slots, and before I realized it I had run out of building slots. I went to build ancillaries to increase my building cap, but I couldn't because you can only place buildings within a certain area away from other buildings, and I wedged myself between a mountain and a river, since I didn't realize that most buildings require large tracts of empty space to function.

It feels less like the game's self-proclaimed challenging difficulty comes from an increasingly difficult horde of scary monsters and more from the government-style bureaucratic red tape. The game does seem like it'd be fun if I stuck with it, but in the end I returned it; I have other games that I want to buy that likely won't frustrate me within the first hour.

Some things you should probably be aware of before purchasing. It's locked at 60fps, you cannot change this in any way, it's core to the game and the game clock is tied to it so forget editing a config file. Developer said they'd change that later in development, but that was 3 years ago, and in the last year the dev hasn't been developing the game due to other life issues, so don't hold your breath.

You can't save the game. It has an autosave feature, and that's it, nothing else. At most you could save&exit, copy/paste your save game file, and restart the game if you want to have a backup...but man, what a hassle just to be able to save a game like normal, right?

People seem to like this game, so I guess there's something good to it. Maybe I'll find out. Thus far all I'm seeing is a game that's not living up to expectations on a basic level.

My conclusion was to pass it up. Here is why:

* It seems that this is a game where you inevitably fail. The goal is to survive some predetermined number of years in a number of villages, however the corruption mechanics makes sure you cannot do that forever, and sooner or later your painstakingly created villages are lost. This is not bad per se, it's just I personally dislike this type of setup
* The "steep learning curve" is mostly because game does not tell you what does what. E.g. What buildings do what, etc, there are some disparate hint windows, that help, but they are not enough. There is no good game manual, no good wiki and no good in-game reference.
* Notification system does not let you easily locate where something happened
* Font is too small if you do not have perfect eyesight. You can scale HUD, but the default option is "RECOMMENDED" so I'm worried that if I scale it, the UI won't fit, or that it will leave less useful space on screen than required for the game to be playable. Have not tried changing the scale though, so this is just a guess.
* Something odd is going with the loading screen. It's displayed 1) when you start the executable 2) when you start new game 3) after you selected starting region 4) when you exit back to main menu (!!!). If you try to screenshot the game, somehow you end up with a screenshot of the loading screen (which may have happened quite awhile ago) instead of the current game position. It looks like the game keeps two screens up (loading screen and the "real" screen) and switching between them but it is not implemented quite properly.

All in all, I believe the game could be fun, but I have so many other games to try, so I'll pass this one up for now.

I *love* citybuilders and population managers. I think [i]Gnomoria[/i] and [i]Banished[/i] are two of my most played games on Steam with about 60 and 30 hours respectively. I put about 40 hours into [i]Dwarf Fortress[/i], and quite enjoyed it. While [i]RPC[/i] desperately wants to be like these titles, it is very far off - in a bad way.

[b]First thing everybody should know is that there is no below-ground mining.[/b] Your world consists of a small-ish 'asteroid' that is one layer of ground thick, floating in space. There are frequent areas of the map that are just 'holes' where you can see the space behind the one-layer thick ground. I am certain that this strange mechanism is a result of limited money/resources/programming ability (idk), and was not intended. [b]The allure of the games cited as inspiration (listed in first paragraph) was largely because you could take 'stuff' out of the ground and organize it above ground! When you take that away, I am significantly less interested.[/b]

[b]You cannot rotate buildings because it would take too much effort to redraw the images.[/b] I get it - prioritize developement, but this is something very basic that needs to be mentioned. It further hints at where this game is going. I would imagine these images could be done in a long weekend, am I right? I am not trying to be harsh, but potential buyers need to be aware of these things.

These are the main two issues I have but there are a myriad of others such as map and individual person custimazation that I will not go into fully.There are also very few buildings at this point. [b]Otherwise the music is quite good, and the artwork is pretty cool.[/b] This game probably was released on Early Access [i]a bit too early.[/i] I got it for half price, and am fine with it because I want to try any and all citybuilders/population managers. 

[b]To my Steam friends: if you haven't played [i]Gnomoria[/i] or [i]Banished[/i] yet, go for those![/b] If you are like me and have exhausted those, this *might* quench your thirst for a bit.

I don't believe any of the issues I put forth will be resolved (I mean its one guy working on this), but if they are, I will alter my review. Thanks for reading,

The Good:
It gives the familiar satisfying feeling of building a base over time.

The overhead god's-eye view and spell system is reminiscent of games like Populous and Black and White, which I really enjoyed in years past.

The Bad:
The graphics are painful even for a pixel game.  That doesn't really bother me, but be warned.

The AI is god awful.  What really got me is you can't even get close to the enemy spawn zones, or your villagers will wander in and attack a some structure for no real reason.  At which point they die instantly.  There isn't currently a system for setting up allowable and forbid-able zones, so when this starts to happen you're pretty much hosed.  It just sucks, and isn't fun.

The "bloodmoon" is a random mechanic that destroys bases outright unless you pepper turrets through them.  The people that are ok with the mechanic have a very specific playstyle: hunker down and turtle.  They will claim bloodmoons are easy to deal with, and they're right... if you only want to play that way.  Again, the developer seems to have a singular vision for what the game is and how it should be played, and if that very specific thing isn't what you're after then tough.  

Painfully repetitive.  There are only four necessary resources: crystals, wood, stone, food.  Water exists but isn't really needed, as you can build wells anywhere they're just slightly slower.  After a couple games you'll realize every map has a handful of spots with all of them, and you settle there.  After that the building, the AI, everything is the same unless you choose to try and play differently.  There isn't anything to adapt to.

There is no real endgame, or goal to reach.  It's tower defense, with the illusion of base building.  Every night the waves get a little harder, and you have expanded your towers to meet the threat.  You can't go out to counter the threat: the game makes it seem like that's a possibility but it's an illusion.   At some point, the difficulty will scale past you and your base will die BY DESIGN.  It's not a skill thing, it's a "the developer literally doesn't want the game to be 'winnable'" thing.  This was the final nail in the coffin for me.  It's not like dwarf fortress or basically any Paradox published game where there isn't a win condition, that doesn't bother me.  It's predetermined you will lose, in a definite way.  The whole point of the game is to get the turn counter to the highest number you can manage before you start over (playing exactly the same way as before).

Last Word:
If the negatives I’ve listed don’t bother you, go for it.  The game is only a few bucks, I don’t regret spending the money.  I just wouldn’t put my recommendation behind it to a friend.  It has some serious flaws.  The part that irked me is that it’s sold like a base-building game… but it isn’t.  Not really.  It’s a tower defense game with a largely irrelevant base-building time waster between waves.

This is an unfinished (Oct. 2018) but ok little city-builder game with a promising "world" level added to the mix. On the basic city scale, the game doesn't do too much new in terms of mechanics, but has great style without doing anything too wrong either. In that sense it's a perfectly fun game, but if you're looking for a city-manager there are simply deeper and more polished options out there, with Banished and Rimworld both being vastly superior. That said, the hierarchical "world" level is where Rise to Ruins has a real chance to set itself apart from the pack. In its current state, your territories can send resources and people to neighboring regions in order to speed colonization- neat but nothing crazy innovative. If the developers push the game in a direction making world level interactions more compelling and interactive, they could really establish a niche for Rise to Ruins. I'm thinking world level events like big corruption battles that are easier or only possible if multiple territories team up to send golems/resources, but the possibilities are vast with the god mechanic as well.

In its current state, the game is not bad. I spent 20+ hours playing it until I got bored, which is pretty damn good for an early access game. That said, I'm giving this the thumbs down for two reasons: 1. negative comments are read more often and 2. there's no reason to play this right now, no matter if you're a fan of the genre or completely new to it. There are just much better options out there for similar price tags. Wait for full release, Rise to Ruins is promising but simply too derivative right now to warrant purchasing.

Issues thus far. Game is EA, so obviously there are going to be issues. The dev is super responsive, my problem is that from some of his responses, some changes haven't come even though he commented about them a year ago. For example, if you accidentally dismantle a building, there's no obvious way to stop this. Researching it shows a comment from the dev stating this function is planned for InDev 18, the game is now on InDev 28.

This really ties into another issue, it's a combination of the game having a small playerbase and the dev probably being indie, there's no updated wiki to look up the game in its current state. The wiki link on the game's official site gives you a WIP page. Trying to look up information on the game leads to posts that span years, making it unreliable on whether or not it's still relevant.

I also have a pretty big issue with the way your buildable area expands. Your walls cut off your "sphere of influence" and you can't build beyond your them. This forces you to tear down walls in order to release your "SOI" in order to build beyond it. This makes it a huge pain in the ass to expand. It's constant leapfrogging your sphere to expand and it gets rather repetitive.

As a final note, props to the dev for being super responsive. This however, leads to another con for me. The dev has indicated some game decisions that I don't really agree with.

For example, I'm in my second game on traditional, it took me some time figuring out how to get things going in my first attempt so I abandoned it after 20ish minutes to restart. My 2nd and current game started a bit hairy, but now I control like 40% of the map and it's just a slow grind at this point. I realize that I'm playing the easiest mode in probably an easy mapset, my issue is that I don't really feel like doing it all over again because of the time investment to build from the ground up again.

I know the dev has made responses as to speeding up the game, my problem is with his responses. The dev has indicated that he wants to add a spell to the game as a temporary buff to your villagers speed instead of just adding a game speed option. My problem with this is that a speed buff is pretty much irrelevant to the issue game speed, they're two entirely different things and the fact that the dev thought this was a response makes me doubt his decision making and the future of the game.

The lack of a game speed option is pretty much deterring me from wanting to try any other maps. Sure, it might be harder and the challenge might be a bit more interesting, but there's just too much sitting and waiting for your villagers to get anything done. From the description: "Rise to Ruins is at heart a godlike village simulator, but it also throws in plenty of familiar game play mechanics from classic real-time strategy and resource management games like Black and White, Settlers, ActRaiser and many others."

I really wish it played that way.

Although the game is indeed a hybrid of several different genres, its implementation of each one is weak.

The village building mechanic: slow and plodding. There's a ton of support structures required for your village, and each one need to be manned by at least one person. Because population growth is slow, nomads aren't frequent, and the speed only goes to 2x before showing you a scary "hey this probably doesn't work" message, growing your city is kind of a boring slog. 

And, since you can't build freely on the map (you're limited to an area around your initial camp, which expands as you build), there's very little variety in the way you approach building a village. There's a bootleg strategy of building a chain of bonfires at the edge of your territory, which extends buildable radius dramatically, but not only is that approach just as slow and boring as the regular one, it also takes up limited building slots, so it feels like a crappy workaround for a crappy system.

At first the mindless slog is tempered somewhat by the introduction of "Corruption," a land-devouring plague. Its mysterious presence, and your slowly building influence meter, builds up anticipation for a Populous-style war: surely the idea is that I growth my village, and thus my influence, so I can use my divine powers to smite the corruption that plagues each region in the game, right?

Well, wrong.

The god system: weak and uninspired. You start off with several different spells in three different categories: loosely speaking you've got harmful spells, helpful spells, and neutral spells. Having said that, most spells are useless. Grab, which moves things around, seems the most interesting but has infrequent usage at best due to the resource drain. Labor Golem, a spell that summons a little stone helper to help move village resources, is invaluable due to the fact that you're always short-handed due to slow village growth (and not, say, any interesting gameplay mechanics).

The rest of the spells seem like they have promise but prove to be worthless. 

Motivate, a spell described as encouraging the regrowth of natural elements, caused an average of 3-4 trees to regrow -- that's nothing compared to your village's needs. 

Meteor, and some fire spell whose name I can't remember (Inferno?), aren't as exciting as they sound. Fires caused by Inferno go out almost immediately. Good luck trying to burn down a forest to keep the enemy from using those resources. In fact, it didn't destroy a single tree the last time I tried. _The fire spell, when cast on a forest, didn't cause a forest fire_.

To cap it all off, even if the spells were powerful and interesting to cast, the only place you'd want to bring down a rain of meteors on, the Corrupted lands, are off-limits to spell casting.

Instead, to deal with the encroaching threat, you...

...you play a tower defense game.

And not a very good one. Turrets have to be built like any other building, use up precious building slots, and have very little differences. There's 5-6 different physical tower types, but in ten hours I only found a use for 2 of them. The rest were of the "like that other turret, except I use stone as ammo!" variety.

The tower defense game has to exist, though, because there's no other way to deal with the Corruption. If you wall it off, they'll just attack your walls, so you need to make an awkward maze of walls and turrets to funnel the enemy though and kill them every night. Except that building the maze, and the turrets, is slow. And when night finally comes, its not even satisfying to watch plodding zombies turn into pincushions.

To sum it all up, much like this review none of the elements in the game really harmonize. The influence system is based on village population, but the spells that use influence are boring and neutered. The Corruption poses an omnipresent threat, but your villagers aren't meant to fight, and the golems you create aren't that interested in it either.

The whole goal of the game seems to be to slowly build-up a village and wait until you have enough villagers so you can colonize another region in the game, but why? The village building is boring. The spell system is boring. The Corruption is interesting, but you can't meaningfully interact with it, so it may as well be boring.

Maybe the game turns amazing during its 12th hour, but I only made it to 11.

In the end, thinking about what Rise to Ruins could have been feels more enjoyable than actually playing it.

It's not a bad game, but it could be a much better game.

At it's heart, it's a little town sim, which is cute enough on its own, but to make things a bit more interesting your town gets regularly attacked by monsters. These monsters follow "tower defense" logic where they don't attack walls and take the shortest route to anything else they can break, so your mission is to build a maze of some complexity, plop down some towers, and behind said maze nurture a society that can upgrade and maintain it.

This is a pretty great concept, but for some reason they thought you'd be up for playing the exact same game like 20-something times. Once you've gotten a self-sustaining society behind the maze, and figured out which towers are pointless(bow, phantom dart and any of the bullet ones, really. Why would I ever build a tower that couldn't shoot over walls?), you've won. So really the only challenge is whether you correctly guess the shortest route and defend that within the first few days, and then you've pretty much won.

Hell, half the citizens' basic needs, like social interaction, you don't even notice because just by existing they satisfy those. Things are automated enough that your only real active control of the world is where to put down buildings, but the AI automation isn't interesting enough to cough up any scenarios as a result(your villagers, for instance, have no personalities, specializations, etc. and only two monsters have abilities beyond "walk towards thing, hit thing.").

It feels like an early access game that slipped through and got released early, because there's just a lack of content and depth.

Not to mention pretty goddamn lackluster tutorializing, it took me until my second year(in-game, not real-time) to figure out that what looked like a bit of UI fancy bordering under the available spells was actually a menu allowing access to more spells.

You can complete challenges to unlock stuff, but they're literally all just "have a +% to do thing in game." None of them change up the gameplay experience or open new options.

There are also some weird AI issues, like how you can organize all village constructor tasks in priorities... except for clearing terrain, which they'll always obsessively do first.

Even just some minor things, like being able to waypoint locations or patrol routes for your rangers and defensive golems would have added a bit of stuff to do. Why does the Medic even exist? I don't think I ever had a villager get injured outside of random weather events, but then they just self-bandaged or went to chill at home for a few seconds and were right as rain. You can't manually order villagers to slaughter livestock, so it's up to the vagaries of the AI whether an animal pen generates any food or not. You can't focus on acquiring iron or gold for gear/trading, respectively, since they're all just random drops from mining generic rock. Storage is completely boned, all storage is available in the same amounts, which means that for relatively rare things, like tools and weapons, you'll never need specialized storage because your stock buildings have enough spare storage for all of it. While for super-common things like rocks, wood and food, you'll always be starved for storage and the buildable storage buildings are almost a waste of your time because they don't give *enough* extra space.

Water seems like an afterthought of a feature, terrain-wise, since it's all hip-deep and wadable, being just a movement speed modifier, and you can effortlessly pave it over. So you can't, for instance, spice things up with stuff like a moat.

I can't really recommend this game, because it could be so much better, and it feels like the dev(s) just didn't want to bother going that last stretch.

It was my fault, as I hadn't realized I had to select those patches of land to tell them to eat. It was my fault for not constructing the corresponding buildings to get them to slaughter the nearby herd. None of this was explained to me. And this is the problem. The game is essentially iron man mode out the box. You can't load earlier saves to fix what becomes an obvious issue once understood. Factoring in the relentless onslaught of enemies by Autumn, and the game railroads you to a certain speed and development despite the various natural disasters and consistent chaos you have to battle through. It's fun to grow and figure out the mechanics, but it's brutal to get it right.

There are obvious problems as well, such as villagers getting stuck on the wrong side of a wall after building. You can't rotate your buildings, which is problematic due to the amount of space allotted to build. If you lose your town center you're effectively screwed, as your building population may require a Keep (much larger town center) to rebuild broken defenses. The enemies are smart enough to scout and find a singular block as an entrance to break into your camp and wreak havoc. However, your own villagers are too afraid to mount any sort of reaction without proper assignment. It makes would could be a fun and interesting learning curve downright tedious and painful to figure out and optimize. If you lose your whole town, you  restart from the very beginning. 

This ultimately makes the game a horde survival base building sim. It's interesting, and I think parts of it are wonderful. It's just not the game I was expecting, and I don't have the patience or time to slog through poorly optimized AI and non-obvious progression. It's commendable, and I hope it continues to improve and develop with time. I would prefer a "slower" more mature game where the village grows to communicate and respond to other towns rather than it evolve into an endless defense against waves of goons.

Ok, so far this is acceptable experience, but here is where it gets really, really ugly.
- No tactical pause. Nothing, really? Can't the deity slow down time or accelerate it's own perception of it to make it look like a tactical pause?
- Loot Chests with description like "Loot box in single player game?!". Inside the game. Breaks immersion AF and is utterly annoying
- non-random campaign maps, world, nothing - every map plays identical
- some weird color scheme that make it hard to figure out ranges or what is actually selected on some maps (orange range of building vs orange ground, green selection circles always on around the toons vs green grass etc)
- aforementioned dissonance between angles of toons vs buildings. It does not go away, it intensifies with more toons
- crowded menu with many small numbers, hard to figure out actions as some are very unintuitive 
- - for example there is no drag and move the map with right click, some actions require multiple extras like saving game config - pressing enter does not do that
- many tiny percentages adding here and there but there is no overview with the list of these and explanation  of what they actually do in game and how they work. What does +5.0% globally to farming do? Is it per map, per world? Do these stack? And WHAT exactly does it do?!
- unable to build decorative terrain, like pavement tiles. Sounds like a minor inconvenience, but wait! There is moar!

So finally, there is the major breaking point of this game. The one that will make all OCD base builders cringe and ragequit. 
As you know, making a perfectly arranged base is what a lot of target audience of such games always aims at.

Not here. Not in this game. Every building is of different size. And they have an extra square around them left for the road. And no, you cannot overlap that square from two different buildings.
And buildings CANNOT BE ROTATED because of reasons.
Dev answer: too much work, would add too much art - yeah, like, everybody knows today sprites can be rotated by the code, you don't need to add 4x as much art. In fact rotating just from N-S to W-E once, would help to alleviate the problem just a bit...

But no. Too lazy.
So you end up with a base that will look like a failed Tetris level with plenty of empty 1x1 or 2x4 squares that you can fill with nothing but some flimsy towers that consume energy. And roads are build one by one. 
Thats right. Every square of wall or road has to be placed manually. More incredibly, every square of wall has to be dismantled manually, if you decide to change the layout.

The amount of extra clicks this game has and inability to make a clear, neat base layout is mindbogling and cringe AF. I've restarted world few times just to re-start base building, until giving up. I've decided to just tear it down later and rebuild (because, of course, you cannot move buildings from one place to another, you have to tear it down and rebuild).

Oof.
I've expected much more from this game, but apparently devs failed to understand the target audience for such titles. And people have been asking for building rotation for years now. So... no.
The two do not align, which may explain why this game failed to attract bigger crowd despite the underlying mechanics being solid and interesting. Honestly, such a pity. With some extra QoL and a fan service for OCD base building players (hint: majority of people playing such games) this could be much better title.

Thoughts about the actual gameplay after 10 hours:

+The pace of the game seems good. Doesn't require reflexes like a RTS would, but also doesn't make you just sit and wait too much.
+In general it shows potential and implies that it has depth and replay value.
+For the most part the UI is clear and easy to use.

+-The lack of in-game tutorial. There is a button for "Watch a tutorial video" and the game gives you some general tips along the way, but they help very little.

-The game offers too little information about things like how many buidlings you need to have in order to have your town survive (farms for food, wells or rain catchers for water etc).
-The time for pixel graphics has come and gone. It actually gets extremely blurry if you zoom in even a little bit (why does it even allow you to do this?).
-The villagers' AI is sometimes bugged and not knowing what their priority is in performing different tasks takes a lot of the fun out of the game.
-Some of the buttons on the UI (assigning villagers to different buildings for example) are WAY too small, considering the next point.
-The mouse pointer moves like it's on a rubber band. The delay ain't that bad, but just enough that it actually gets really annoying to try and aim at some of the smaller buttons.

It's these last two points that made my review negative. Feels like something that wouldn't bother a normal person, but some of the buttons are really small and the rubber banding mouse ain't helping.

And in case anyone gets to read this before the fanboys downvote this into oblivion (as they do to all negative reviews): I'm not saying not to buy it. But I am suggesting to keep an eye on the development for a while before doing so.

Other reviews complain about sudden jumps in difficulty but I suspect this is mostly because it is hard to determine your current status. This is both boring and frustrating.

(2) It is difficult to find good information on any of the buildings or game mechanics.
Does a static tower shoot through curtain walls? (No). Why do golems wander so far and patrol where they do? How does courier or migration work? Even basic functions like locating how to designate an area to dig a hole is non-intuitive hidden in a separate sub-menu. For some reason "walls" are not listed under the "defense" category but lightning rods are. How much food does a fully upgraded farm generate? The hidden pathing mechanics of the monsters including spectres and fire elementals which have un-announce mechanics specific to them. It is difficult to design a tower defense if there is a general lack of information about the towers, defenses, and monsters.

I really really really wanted to like this game.  I love the Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress, ONI, etc type games, and I've always liked tower defense games, so I found the concept of this game quite intriguing.  And there is a lot of game here... lots of buildings and upgrades, interesting world map concept and global perks/xp, migrating people from your starting town outwards to start new towns... all this plus tower-defense style planning.  What's not to like?

Alas, it never really came together for me in a way that was actually fun.  You can tell there's a lot going on under the hood, but the UI is frustratingly opaque and uninformative; I frequently found myself unable to get the information I wanted, or unable to do anything with the information once I had it.  There's a ton of buttons, windows, menus, and lists, but there's no tech tree or tutorial to unlock them in a logical order.  So the initial experience is a little overwhelming, but I rapidly got to the point of knowing which buildings were important, which towers were needed, and what order to build things in, at which point... there was nothing to do.  I found myself just sitting there, watching the game flicker by at a fast speed, occasionally upgrading buildings/towers, and wondering what to do next.  There are no real goals, no obvious way to interact with the world, no significant advantage in expanding; nothing to really plan or strategize or think about.  Even bad things that lead to people dying can be mostly ignored, since your people are almost instantly replaced by nomads with no discernible penalty that I could detect (there probably is a penalty of some sort... but that gets back to the opaque UI).   I rapidly ran out of interesting decisions to make and ended up just marking time until I could migrate out more people to create a carbon copy of my village all over again.  Which after the first few times, really isn't very interesting or challenging anymore.

And a personal pet peeve.... dogs barking.  You eventually get dogs to join your village.  And they bark.  Non-stop.  Literally hours of a background sound track of bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark.  With no way that I could find to turn off their barking or get rid of them, without also turning off the "something important happened!" type sounds.  This won't bother everyone, but for me it was the final straw.

While I am not reccommending this game, it is mostly due to its standard price, which I think is highway robbery.  I picked this game up on sale for a couple of dollars, and have had a blast for nearly 20 hours.  That being said, if I had paid $10.99 for the game (current prices in maple syrup dollars), I'd feel pretty ripped off / let down.

- Steep-ish learning curve.  Things arn't so insurmountable that you'll need a wiki, but there is enough going on that you will fail a few times figuring it all out.  Really embraces the "loosing is fun" mentality.
- Runs on a toaster (sort of...)
- Early gameplay is incredibly addictive.  I have felt like going for just "one more day" multiple sessions now.
- Scratches that "Dwarf Fortress" itch a little.  Though, this is more tower defence than it is DF.
- Lots of incentive to try again (rewards for "god experience" make the game easier, etc). 
- Once you actually figure out the intended build order, this game is actually quite chill / relaxing. 

Cons:
- "Combat" is shallow.  You exploit enemy pathing to succeed as long as possible.  The main stratedgy is to buld long winding paths to herd mobs near your towers.  Classic tower defence mechanics.  However, there is a limited set of resources to exploit (technically, just "energy", crystals, stone, and wood), and almost all the tower feels exactly the same as one another (simply with different firing rates).  You CAN build soldiers or golems, but it's mostly pointless as you can simply rely on the towers.
- Building Limits are your greatest enemy.  Until you figure out HOW the game demands you play, you're often fighting against the building limits.  My early games often hit a brick wall when I was told I could not build any more buildings without performing a Capital building upgrade (or building an expansion building).  There is a proper building path, and it leaves very little room for experimentation.
-  Due to the building limits, Food and Water become your second greatest foes.   Early on, before you realize the "gotchas", you'll doom your village simply by building a wooden gate (which counts as a building for some reason).  Again, once you realize the intended building path, things become trivial to manage.  However it completely sucks away any sort of creativity in playstyle (unlike DF).
- Yes, gates are considered buildings under the building limit.  No, the fences the gates are attached to are not part of the limit.  Yes, this is quite stupid.
- Your god powers feel... underwhelming.  I felt that the meteor, etc, were mostly useless.  I ended up using three pwoer consistently  my near 20 hours playing this game:  the growth spell, the labour golem spell, and most importantly the pick sh*t up spell (gotta find those mysterious keys!).  The other... 15ish spells?   Never bothered with them.  Sure, maybe they have some viability to mix up play, but those three spells carried my ass through 4 regions with ease.  I really feel these should be unlocked somehow, rathan given away at the start.
- The "win" condition is to settle in each biome of the map.  When you're starting out, this seems impossible - the blight comes so quickly!  My people are starving!  But then, after a few false starts, you figure out the intended play style, and fire off your first volley of settlers to the next region.  Perhaps you also ship off some starting cargo.   Bam, headstart.  You'll be up and running in no time, probably taking half the time to get to the same level of development.  Then you repeat this process, ad nausium, until you "win".  You can't "win" a region either.  The blight will slowly overtake the region map, forcing you to abandon it regardless.  There is barely a difference between regions (other than avaiable resources).  It becomes pretty dull once you hit the 15-20 hour mark IMO.

I know I spent quite a bit of time ragging on it, but I don't want you to think its a bad game.  I actually think it's pretty good!  It's just not worth $10.  I understand it is an indie product, and that its in early access, but it's not even as polished as the old single z-level version of Dwarf Fortress.  If you can get this for $5 or less, you'll have a great time, and get your fatass dirty dollars worth.  But for all that is holy, don't buy this at full price!

Normally I make fairly in-depth reviews, but I'm gonna skip that with this. There's a lot of fairly interesting design choices here and maybe a framework for a good game, but a city builder/sim this is not. This is a tower defense (despite what the game creator says) where you fight absurdly bloated HP monsters with very little actual strategy.

It's cool that there's a huge handcrafted island with different areas, but they all pretty much play the same.  There's mechanics to outfit your villagers with armor and weapons, but this is pointless as villagers barely fight and will instantly die later in the game.

The game, while not graphically ugly, makes it hard to identify what buildings are which without clicking on them. It feels like only the early game portion of this game was actually finished, and instead of introducing stronger towers, walls, golems, magic items or heroes, you just pick up enemies and drop them in instant death pits.

Honestly, I like the concept of this game, as a colony game with spells, but there are too many negatives for me to recommend. 

This game is incredibly slow to play through.  Each day takes an hour, and your colonists take FOREVER to build and deliver resources.  If you queue up 5 buildings, it can take literal days for your colonists to deliver and construct them.  Priority setting on buildings seemed inconsistent at best regarding what order my colonists would construct things, causing them to finish things even slower it seemed.

Colonist AI is atrocious.  They will frequently wander close to the corruption and die because they wanted to pick up some items.  There's no way to set an area for them to not wander around in.  Other times they'll run up to an enemy that will kill them in a few hits (fire elementals).  You just have to know that this will happen in your playthrough, because the game doesn't let you control your colonists in any way to reliably save them from themselves.

Worker management is tedious and unhelpful.  When workers are idle, they don't do other tasks that need to be done.  If you assign workers to make ballista bolts until storage is full, once they finish they'll just sit there.  So now if you want to be efficient, you have to unassign them from the bowyer building and place them somewhere else, and then reassign them when you want more.  I can't believe more people don't complain about how confusing the slots system is for buildings.  For example, a single farmer will comfortably take care of 3-4 farms without idle time.  But if you build 3-4 farms, there's enough slots that you can assign like 12 farmers.  If you assign those 12 farmers, 10-11 of them will be completely idle as you really only should have assigned 1 or 2 farmers at most.  The game doesn't warn you that you have idle villagers either.  The ranger's outpost is another example of this problem.  If you want to have most of your workforce being idle, throw a bunch of people in there, because rangers are completely useless in this game.

Water carriers don't prioritize farms in this game.  I've had fountains full of water and my farms are dry.  You know why?  Because my guys assigned to water distribution are delivering water to houses that are already nearly full of water and in no danger of running low anytime soon.  

Most spells are garbage.  There's lightning, fire, magic missiles etc.  You can drop a useless meteor on some enemies and do a little damage.  But why should I use any of these when they're horribly inefficient and I can instead pick up and drop an enemy into a building that kills them in one hit.  Though that ends up being horribly tedious as well.  There's the grab spell, but you can't pick up more than 1 thing at a time.  You wanted to help build?  Then you have to tediously pick up and drop 1 resource at a time onto a building under construction, when they usually take 32 resources MINIMUM for the lowest tier.  And for some stupid reason, you're penalized if you're not quick about it.  If you hold onto a resource or an enemy for too long, your mana starts to drain, so you better be quick!  This game just loves to hurt your wrists.

On the other side, there are 3-4 incredibly OP spells.  Harvest is ridiculous, and will net you 100 wood/stone or more with every cast. Something that would take your colonists a literal day to chop/mine is now done in seconds.  You don't even need to build a mine or a tree harvester building with this spell.  Holy Potatoes and the regenerate land spell combined with harvest means you don't really need farms either, they're that OP.

Don't even bother trying to do animal husbandry.  The breed rate and butcher rate is so ridiculously slow that you might need 10 animal pens if you actually wanted to use them to feed your colony.  But again, you shouldn't even bother tbh.  Just use Holy Potatoes and get all the food you need.  Even if you don't use that spell, just eating raw vegetables from your farms works perfectly fine.

There's a general lack of information in the UI.  What's the difference between raw meat and cooked meat?  I couldn't tell you.  My colonists will eat both as far as I can tell.  Do the animals I keep in my animal pens and chicken farms eat my vegetables or are they grass eaters?  Beats me.  Are eggs and boiled eggs from my chicken farm any better for my colonists than raw vegetables?  I have no idea.  None of that is explained anywhere that I can tell.  

The lack of a tutorial when you start the game.  I think I understand the game clearly enough now, but honestly this game could have used a longer tutorial when first selecting an area and playing through it.  I see enough reviews that this is clearly an issue.

The tower/defensive balances in this game are not well balanced.  Golems are straight up better than defensive towers.  They're cheaper, mobile, don't require ammunition, don't require any sort of maze to build (which can be walked through by some enemies anyways), and can help you offensively if you build lights right up against the corruption.  Literally building mass golems is the best strategy I've come across.  There's also armor and weapons you can equip your colonists to fight with, and an outpost building you can use them to patrol with.  Why is this even in the game?  Colonists are so fragile in this game, you can't control them, and you generally need them doing other stuff that I can't fathom why the dev thought anybody would want to send them to the front-lines, especially when you can't readily replenish them.

There's also no way to technically be offensive against the corruption in this game.  You may happen to have some golems wander close enough to the corruption that they'll attack something and draw some aggro, but there's no way to specifically order your golems, or even colonists, to attack and clear out an area, which is quite sad.

Speaking of that, colonist spawn rates is another issue that slows this game down.  It's entirely random when you have nomads join you.  Apart from nomads, you can also gain population through childbirth and by buying workers to join your colony.  The problems?  Childbirth is as infrequent as nomads and quite often the children will not make it through childbirth.  Nothing you can do about that.  And you're lucky if you actually see more than 1 worker every 3-4 days (2-3 real life hours) for sale.  They're that infrequent.  Actually, because those workers show up at the merchant station, its actually beneficial to pick up your merchants and kill them so that more slots are available for workers to show up.  No penalty for doing that.  That's how ridiculous it is.  I can have an abundance of food, housing space, water, and defenses, and I'm still being bottlenecked in population by something completely out of my control.

The pause button doesn't let you scroll around the map, or view things.  It throws a screen in front of you so you can't see or interact with anything.  I just wanted to pause and take a look at a battle or plan out some building placement, but screw me I guess.

Allow me to start this review off by saying that this is the first review I've written in perhaps 6 years. However, please do not consider this to be a bad thing, as I honestly believe this game has great potential. I'm leaving this review in the hopes that the developers see it and perhaps take my recommendations into consideration.

Rise to ruins appears to me as if it is a spiritual successor to Towns, an incomplete colony sim from 2012. You build a village, manage its villagers by assigning jobs, and building towers to defend the walls. It's fun, what can I say? However, I cannot recommend this game for many reasons in its current state. I will list them out below.

1.) First of all, there are grammar issues. A few missed commas and miss-capitalization here and there. Easily fixed I believe.

2.) Disaster Response: In this game, there is no way to respond to disasters at all. If anything happens to any of your villagers, their first reaction is to run scared. There is no way to prevent this. You can't change how villagers react to dangers, even if you equip them with a weapon (as far as I could tell). You also can't prioritize jobs (like chopping trees or mining stone or manufacturing items) nor can you issue direct orders to your villagers, so anytime there is a stay zombie, there is nothing you can do about it until someone suddenly decides they want to fight or the zombie wanders into the range of a turret.

3.) Balance issues: I believe there are many, many balance problems here. This will be the meatiest entry. First of all, there are wayyyy too many jobs and not enough villagers. I do not understand why the villager who smelts iron can't also smith the armour & weapons, at least at the beginning of the game? Why can't the villager who fetches water from the rain collector or water purifier also bottle the water? It makes no sense to me. My villages consistently grind to a halt as I wait for more hands to show up or be born so I can hire a new waymaker. This is also another thing, I think that the rate at which villagers multiply should be increased, as in a 6 hour game (where my main source of incoming villagers were nomads), I saw one birth and still had to wait for them to grow up. On top of this, limiting buildings (their number and positions) is more of an inconvenience than anything. In the same 6 hour game, I never got to construct a single building in regards to crystal collection. Disasters need to be scaled down. After reaching day 5, I had two meteor showers and one earthquake in one day, which completely destroyed my village.

All in all, I really like this game, like I said, I think it has great potential, it just needs to be worked on still. As is usual with these types of reviews, I will change my recommendation when these issues get fixed. Otherwise, great work so far!

So this game has been updated, and i've been asked to check the game out again since there is now more content, and this does TECHNICALLY qualify as an early version of the game, rather than simply being a tech demo as it originally was, dumped on steam with no warning that the game wasn't practically playable any more than starcraft 2 with only command centers and scv's would be.

But i'm not impressed. My problems with this game comes down to 

 - Terrible "village management"
 - Sketchy bussiness practice, not necessarily malignant, but the dev is inexperienced and it shows
 - Lack of direction
 - There is no way to make interesting maps (All current ones are garbage)
 - Even at 10€ the game is heavily overpriced

I don't want to go into little bugs and irritants, although they are not in short supply, this is early access and these are expected, but the above problems aren't something you can fix with a little patch, they require major reworkings of the game or the way the development operates.

By far the biggest issue here is the way new villagers are aquired; the game borrows the double dumbass approach of towns where you will only reproduce if your people are happy AND your people will only be happy if they aren't doing anything. I really didn't want to add this sentence but if you look in the comments for this review it's obvious i'm going to get called on it if i don't so yes, technically you CAN aquire new citizens even at 0 happiness, but the odds of that happening are so abysmally low, i've played 4 games now and i've seen 1 new person appear at <25 happiness, so it doesn't matter.

This is made far worse by the game's approach to combat. I expect combat to change a lot as new features are planned for it, but it is still taking the approach of high volatility combat; you're going to lose people defending your home. Compare this to Towns and Dwarf Fortress; in towns you also have this stupid villager approach to population growth, but you're very unlikely to lose people in combat, so it doesn't completely shut down your village even if you're frequently in combat. Dwarf fortress has frequent, massive genocides with scores of dead characters, but population growth is tied to the value of all items your fort owns, and looting enemies gives you lots of weapons, armor and clothes of good value, so you typically get lots of new migrants coming in to refill the ranks of your military.

This game has you attacked about every 30 seconds right now, there is practically no breathing room, and it starts immediately. The game seems more like an RTS than a village sim, but with an extremely slow process of replenishing your forces. This could work in the same ways as custom maps for starcraft and warcraft have done, which was awesome, but when you can't expand your population you're just stuck, unable to do anything.

Tying happiness to idling is another total failure for the game, especially with the constant aggression. You basically turn the whole game into ballancing workload vs free time; too little workload and you won't be able to build the defenses, too much workload and you never get enough people. This could work as a component to the game, but it just becomes the sole focus, and all you end up doing is unassigning and reassigning people in a neverending circle of tedius micromanagement.

Speaking of tedius micromanagement, the villagers are terrible at carrying out tasks efficiently. If you order too many houses/defenses/farms (read: more than 2) they'll start building the first house, then when it's halfway done, they apparently switch to the next, with just a few people working on the first. The result is a collage of unfinished structures littering your town, and if you're building defenses while they're being attacked, the builders will drop their materials to fight, then carry them of to the wrong building, leaving a single unfinished tower for up to 20 minutes was the worst i had, with the little idiots running back to pick up their wood, then drop it as a zombie got close, run over to punch the zombie, then pick up the wood and haul it to another tower under construction. (I queued 4 towers, silly me)

This isn't really a big issue to work around, just don't queue up constructions, right? Sure, but this is more micromanagement on top of giving builders their mandatory vacation time, and on top of the next issue:

Villagers apparently gather resources from completely random places. This means if you're building something in one place and you assign them to gather wood/rocks nearby, they'll gather it there, but if you then build the next building somewhere else (Why would anyone want to keep their farms and defenses seperate...?) you have to unassign where to gather resources, or the idiots will run halfway across the map to chop down a tree, instead of the one assigned right next to them. 

All this combined means you don't spend your time organizing defenses, planning your town or anything you'd expect from this game, you're just babysitting these idiotic villagers; go chop here, don't chop there, don't be a builder, don't mine there, mine here, be a builder, don't be a farmer, etc. etc. and this is what the game is; it takes hours to build anything because of this nonsense, and you need to leave the game running without building anything to get new villagers.

The other major issue with this as a village sim is that there are no different resources; just food and construction materials. Wood and stone are just different colours; no buildings/tools/tech needed for extraction, take the same time, trees don't regrow, what's the point?

The game's bussiness practice also smells bad. The game was initially kickstarted successfully, and IMMEDIATELY after that it was dumped on early access, despite being nothing more than an abysmal tech demo; no combat, just farms and houses forever; 30 minutes and the game ran out of things to do. My problem with this is how eager the dev is for cash. Why wasn't the kickstarter enough to at least make a functional game before throwing it out here? He'll happily charge full price for a tech demo, and the "game" has even been on sale. I hate old sayings, but "Don't sell the skin before shooting the bear" seems apt for once.

The other problem the dev has is the game's lack of focus. This game is NOT on early access to get feedback, because there are so many features missing it's practically impossible to give any worthwhile feedback. What the dev seems to want is ideas for where to take his game, and early access is a terrible place for that. Maybe you want a village sim and this turns into an RTS? Well then, jokes on you. It's impossible to satisfy everyone, but you're still charging them for it. Like i wrote at first, the game has elements of an RTS and a village sim as the dev advertises both on the store page and here: http://retropixelcastles.com/index.php?/page/key_features.html but they don't work together. You can't have the volatility of an RTS combined with the slow growth of a village sim; one has to dominate. The game also touts this "inevitable failure" part, as if it has any benefit; If you're building a village you want to see it grow and expand; what's the point of that if the village doesn't matter and you're just playing for high score? I don't mind the "see how long you can last" thing, but its fun in an RTS, where you build things only because of their immediate value to your survival, not in a village sim. 

Apparently we're supposed to unlock stuff after we die, because grinding for necessary unlocks is everyone's favorite thing about videogames.

The game also claims to be "unique" which is nonsense; stronghold and majesty has done "defend and grow village" over a decade ago, and MUCH better. 

TL;DR: This is an RTS where all you can build is farms, houses and towers, and you can't control or replenish your units.
