I really tried to like this game on Survival in its current state which is probably the last state. It is "the way the game is meant to be played", as the description says. Yet, as one of the streamers noted, "the game requires a very strong attention to detail". Moreover, it punishes you when you are not attentive.

Some players like unfair punishment, and this game may be for you if you are one of them. It has a good technical state for an indie game and has a lot of fun mechanics. I get a cursor problem in fullscreen, yet the game can be played in a window to mitigate that. There are pretty visual effects. The price is not steep.

It does not have saves. Bro, in 2024 even Dwarf Fortress has saves.  The game does have an emergency pause. This is not a pause I want for a strategy game. I want to carefully examine the situation without a rush. The game has a customly designed pixel font which is very small and hard to read. I consider all this as a form of punishment.

About gameplay.

Can you just spam your spells? No, the game punishes you with a constant drain of "total faith", and you have to help your villages to maintain it. There were a few other impressive actions you have to learn, I know they exist (based on my total faith), yet I have not discovered them yet. On the other side, you get a massive faith decrease when your villager dies.

Do you think you can get food flow from farms? No, farmers are only good at picking up the wild crops. You have to regrow the crops via magic. The information like this is quite hard to come by. People say, "Just build 10 farms". No, you cannot do that on Survival and get profit.

These two mechanics are the worst because even if you backup your savefile by copying it, you cannot win against constant resource drain. 

There are some other scenarios when a save backup would help. I sent your villagers to build something near the front line. They decide to attack a graveyard instead. A squad of elite enemy units teleports and destroys my villagers. My total faith is 200 after that, I cannot cast most spells, including the food spell. 

The guide says, "to move enemy back build the wall, the line of catapults, the line of fire pits, repeat". I believe this may work. The point is I'm not really interested in repeating this process 10 times to clean the map.

The description says, "Survival has a steep learning curve". No, it does not have a learning curve. You learn to reset the world after each mistake because mistakes are not recoverable. The guides on the game and YouTube walkthroughs are mediocre.

Probably if I have only game to play, I play and learn all its quirkiness and maybe even master it. But today I just switch to another game.

1. The graphics never stop flickering on any graphics setting.
2. Basic controls are awkward, imprecise and essential short cut commands to delete structures or cancel orders are not explained anywhere and have to be experimented with to find (or looked up via an internet search).
3. Basic resource management is automated, but makes little sense. Most egregious example: raw food is the used both for planting and feeding your people; they will eat their "seed" food with no warning, making farms cease to produce food; once this occurs it is too late to fix since they will be starving and continuously eat everything they grow.
4. Game progress is very slow (and requires you to constantly alt-tab to look up controls), so by the time you figure out reasons 1 through 3, you won't have done anything in appreciable in game, but it will be too late to get a refund through steam.

I love simulation games, but am sad that I spent money on this one. I hope this helps others avoid the same frustration.

Also, you can't pause the construction of walls, meaning your Builders will always have it as a priority on their list, even if you don't want those Crylithium Curtain Walls built because your Crystal Harvestry got destroyed by a random Specter last night and you want to spend your remaining Crylithium on charging your Essence Collectors (you can't stop them, and they will spend all of your Crylithium on those walls and you will lose because your towers will have no charge)

As for the tower-defense aspect, it's just a matter of time before you discover that spamming Ice Golems and Ice Bolt towers is the only way to survive the later waves. You can't determine target priority on towers, and Ice is the damage type that no monster in the game resists, as well as dealing bonus damage to Fire Elementals. There isn't any strategy to placing towers beyond the basics (line them up behind walls and make a maze). All in all, it's a fantastic concept, but the game spreads itself thin among its many interacting systems and fails to convey critical information when it should be immediately known. Its cracks will show the more you try to experiment, but even if you're fine with sticking to the meta, you'll still find yourself at the short end of the stick when you eventually fail to notice a lose condition the game doesn't do much to help you keep track of.

This is a mixed review:

The game's premise, mechanics, graphics, resource management, etc are all fantastic, and build the premise for a great game.

Unfortunately, as you get further into the game, is when the bugs become apparent, and you run into severe difficulty spikes.  For example, if you try to clear the corruption, you'll eventually get to the point having a building on a tile right next to corruption may not clear it (or clear it very slowly).  You'll also be able to handle almost everything the game throws at you, until suddenly the game decides to 4x the spawn rate and health of every enemy.  Maybe I'm playing the game wrong, and you're not supposed to push out?  Reading other reviews, I guess I'm supposed to migrate at some point, however it's difficult to know when, given the difficulty suddenly spiking beyond control.

Then comes the bugs.  Early game, you'll be able to build lots of things each day.  As your village grows, you get more builders, miners, etc, you begin to accomplish significantly less each day.  For example, even with plenty of resources, including resources nearby, top-tier roads, I'm still only able to build about 3 buildings per day.  Or I might have 20 waymakers (road builders), but no roads seem to be built for days on end.  Don't get me started on rations, I can't seem to get my cooks to make them ever.

I really wish I could like this game.  I remember enjoying it a bit when I first bought it, then I stopped playing.  Life got in the way, I didn't have as much time.

This game punishes you harshly for lack of knowledge.  If you do not understand exactly how all the game mechanics function, you will lose.  There is very little chance of learning your way to victory on the fly.  The tutorial gives random tips that help, a little, but I find that I've already figured out the (very basic) information provided by the time they appear.

The UI is awful.  Selecting villagers is an exercise in complete randomness.  Alerts will tell you when something happens with a particular villager, but good luck figuring out where.  Same thing with monster attacks and buildings being destroyed: these are important things, but figuring out where they are happening so you can respond is down to luck.  You must know what buildings you have where at all times or you will spend valuable time searching for the problem.  There are many spells that could be useful, but often they are dependent on timing and with so few ready spell slots you often have to go searching through a list of meaningless icons to find what you need.

There's also the issue of countering attacks.  There is no clear in-game way to tell which towers are effective against which enemies.  You can deduce, over time, that bow towers aren't effective against skeletons, almost everything will target a specter but few things actually do damage, and fire elementals are both tanky and will light everything - people, buildings, everything - on fire and set you back for days at a time.  Fire elementals have no effective counter I've found: probably keeping a magic tower up long enough to do some expensive upgrades would kill them faster, but since they can burn everything they'd just wipe out the tower in response.

There is no good source of all this missing information that I've found.  Bits and pieces are in various places, but otherwise you're on your own.  It's an exercise in frustration.

Game is a simple god-sim citybuilder mixed with tower defence.

TL;DR: It does some things right and can possibly entertain you for a while, if you like the premise. At the moment I cannot recommend it, because of some issues.


Interface:
First and foremost, the interface is rather clunky to use and doesn't do a particularly great job utilising the screen space and presenting the information to you.

The icons for many of the ressources are almost or entirely identical to each other (with only a colour difference) it does a poor job of presenting the information you need to you.

Many of the building categories only contain a few buildings and some are overfilled or have sub-categories, making finding the building you want to place take that extra bit of time, that slowly gets a bit annoying.

The job assignment list is unsorted, which makes it surprisingly unhandy when you need to move people around. Each entry also takes up far too much space on the screen because of the way it is presented -- Every single job could easily be on screen at all time if this were redesigned.

It may just be me, but integrating a "please give me a good steam review" notice into the main menu seems a bit shady.

It also doesn't help that some of the less user-friendly (and sometimes frustrating) gui choices have been confirmed by the dev to be intended so as to force the player into playing the way the dev feels it should be played.


No pausing:
An important deal-breaker for me is that when you press pause, the game locks you out of it. Only thing you can do while paused is look at some statistics. The reason for this is, according to the dev, that you should feel like you are a part of the world, so if time isn't running, you should not be allowed to see the world.

To me it is simply an unnecessary restriction that makes the game less fun when you are not allowed to watch your city and the map around it while paused -- no need to be able to interact with anything, simply letting the player watch his creation while paused should always be a thing in citybuilding games.

This is a game where you build a town made up of a lot of buildings of varying sizes often in areas where space is at a premium -- buildings you aren't allowed to rotate to make them fit better. So taking your time to count tiles and figure out where things can fit can take a fair bit of time. Maybe your current city is doomed, so you need to figure out how to improve your city layout before starting a new game. Whatever the reason, a pause that simply lets you see the map and nothing else would change it from frustrating to fun.


Game world:
Right now there is a single world map for you to play on. The world map is made up of a lot of playable chunks that offer the actual game areas. This works as intended to give the player a good selection of maps with varying difficulty.

Sadly, the game does not let you reset a single world map piece, but rather forces you to either delete the entire world or keep playing with already played maps locked off. Locked off, because if you won, there is no need to return and if you lost, the map is impossible to reconquer since it has been overrun by enemies.

It would be a big improvement to be able to selectively cleanse specific of the playable maps. 


Gameplay - city management:
The gameplay is rather straightforward citybuilding and ressource management (food/water/population/housing) mixed with god mechanics where you can cast spells every now and again. It works pretty well, even if the economy could need a fair bit of balancing.

Spells don't always work as intended (and I am not talking about the intended mishaps), which can be frustrating. For example when you cast a spell that is supposed to regrow forests, food, and crystals in the immediate area, sometimes a lot of things regrow and sometimes next to nothing does. It makes the spells feel less like reliable god powers and more like a lottery, which makes you feel less like a god and more like a sky charlatan at times. Maybe this is intended.


Gameplay - city economy:
A lot of micromanagement is needed to make sure your economy is balanced correctly (like having enough ammo/food/water stockpiled. This is made into a bit of a problem by the game not telling you which items despawn and which don't. So if you overproduce items resulting in things being left on the ground, many of them will simply dissolve -- and some will not (or do so very slowly). No way to know which items can safely be left outside or for how long.

This could be alleviated by the default "how many to keep producing" setting for buildings being set to "how many can fit into the storage space of the building itself". That some items take up 1 storage amount per item and other items taking up 1 storage amount per 10 or 20 items makes it a bit of a chore to fiddle with at times.


Gameplay - combat:
Combat is a bit of a mess, which I think is intended. It would however be nice if you have slighlty better control.

Your non-combat villagers either run away or fight. It is a bit of a crapshoot whether or not they do one or the other and sometimes they alternate back and forth every second or run directly into groups of enemies when running from whatever they feel they need to run from. Would be nice if you could tell them to either attack or run away always, since the mix just about ensure that they die if they ever go near an enemy.

Your combat troops will walk around as they please, and you can not tell them to guard specific areas even if every single enemy follows the same path (with only ghosts being able to fly through walls). So often your guards will be miles away for no reason.

Your towers seem to fire on whatever they please (usually first thing to get within range) with no regard as to whether or not the thing it fires can do any damage (ghosts are nearly impervious to non-magic attacks, so if a ghost slowly drifts into range of your wall of non-magic towers before a group of zombies arrive then the zombies will get to chew on whatever they like. Magic towers use a somewhat limited ressource to attack, so at times you only want to use them when it is needed.

There may be a hidden priority to the targeting, and if so it isn't clear how or if it works.

Having the option to tell towers to prioritise certain targets over other or even to ignore some types would improve the tower defense portion of the game a lot. 


Gameplay - winning:
There is no way to win yet.

You can lose a map by getting overrun, which then makes it impossible for you to do anything on it, and you can "win" a map by cornering the enemy and getting the upper hand. But there is no way to get to a "you win" screen.

Whether or not this is a good thing is up to the player.


Graphics:
A lot of attention has gone into making the world seem alive and it shows. The art style is by no means beautiful but it works well enough and all the little animations and things like build stages for every building helps and makes you appreciate it after a few hours. The art for the buildings could be improved a lot if the differences were more distinct -- they all basically use the same building blocks. 

While all buildings have its own art, the difference between (for example) your mining facility and your lumber shack or a house is not immediately obvious, so if you want to click a specific building, you will often click around for a while until you find it. It should not be necessary to memorise the building layouts in order to recognise them. Some buildings are drawn much better and include a lot of things unique to that building, making them instantly recognisable.

All in all, the graphics could be improved but grow on you the longer you play.


Conclusion:
The game has a promise, but as it stands now it feels too rough around the edges for me to recommend.

It works as a relaxing town builder, with some danger to keep things interesting, but it advertises itself as a tower defense and doesn't work as one. You see the big mechanic in the game is corruption, which spreads moderately across the map and spawns enemies and contains buildings. If you refuse to surrender 11/12 of the map to the corruption and go on the offensive to box in the corruption, you can also 'win'. This is actually very fun and somewhat challenging until you succeed in trapping it in a corner, unable to finish it off due to permanent corruption tiles, the number depending on the day you're currently on. Then that's it, you've won. The game is now a sandbox city builder, a sort of purgatory you didn't sign up for as you wonder if you should just start a new game or wait to see if they ever spawn enough to grow a bit.

So ok, let's play it as the tower defense game it's meant to be played as. The developer clearly has a specific idea of how the game is meant to be played, sitting down and building a tower defense maze. Oh yeah, and if you do what the game intends and build a maze, **if it's too long of a maze the AI will just attack your walls** and bust through in a twisted gotcha. If you have too much surface area you'll get punished for it. You better have several mazes, but your maximum number of buildings is limited. A bit of a slap in the face there dev. Glad I don't follow your rules and rush the corruption, I feel sorry for people who just want to play the game normally. 

So if you play your own way you'll find the game unrewarding, and if you play the game the way the dev so clearly wants than he pulls the carpet out and kills ten hours of your work. Those tower defense mechanics might have been good enough to be fun, but even on the hardest difficulty the first 10 days are far too easy, and then it suddenly becomes far too hard the moment your first building breaks and the undead crash through the rest. Speaking of days though...

The game is split into segments of a day, with each day lasting a real-life hour. In campaign/worldmap mode, which you will play if like me you like progression, there are 36 maps. Currently the win condition is to survive 100 days on each map. This is not possible on any map unless you cheese the game or play easy. Finding the minimum playtime to win gives us 1 hour X 100 (number of cycles needed to win a map) X 36 total maps = 3600 hours. So don't bother trying to 'win' the world-map.

Play it if you like zoning out or building and are ok with being slapped around by the dev's 'gameplay decisions', or are good enough to cheese the game. Otherwise, pass.

This is a tough review to write - because this is my favorite game of 2019, save one, and I still can't honestly recommend it in its current form. It has so much potential to be exactly the game I'm looking for - a version of Settlers that Ubisoft hasn't screwed up. But it's not there yet, in infuriating ways.

Pros:
- Good soundtrack,
- Game has a dark sense of humor regarding villager death,
- Even at night, during a rain storm, the environment is bright enough to see,
- The building UI is intuitive,
- The God-points system adds an interesting Rogue-like element,
- The learning curve is steep, but not too steep.

Cons:
- The villager AI is moronic,
- Pathing can get to be a real problem if corruption spreads in an inconvenient manner,
- Relying on Nomads and children aging to adulthood is great in theory, but you can quickly become completely overrun by monsters without enough population to defend yourself,
- Some of the perks from God-points rely on such random occurrences that their usefulness is greatly diminished,
- Tying influence (mana) to population can make surviving long enough to cast multiple spells impossible,
- Building priority doesn't mean anything useful,
- There's no way to tell individual villagers what to do,
- The game really, really either needs a "no, I really mean it, build this right the hell now" option, or a lightning bolt I can use to punish villagers for their stupidity,
- Dropping the game's difficulty makes the game way too easy,
- Peaceful is, quite possibly, the most boring experience I've ever come across,
- Some of the comedy/pop-culture names can get a bit... racisty.

So, no - I cannot recommend this game, at this time. But it's my favorite game that came out this year, and I suspect that I will probably spend many, many more hours beating my head against the wall that is the ridiculous AI. Tl;dr this game is a losing simulator. You will unavoidably lose. There is literally no way to win. This isn't a "gid gud" scenario, you will lose every time, by design.

I refrained from writing a review for this game because I didn't want to hinder its progress, just in case the dev wanted to change the direction of the game. It's very sad that I have to say no, but I will explain underneath the reasons why.

The game is really cool until you realize what the gameplay cycle is. I haven't played it in a while but I saw some comments and it seems it's still the same.

The game isn't difficult. It's impossible by design. I don't mind difficult games. But the whole formula of this game is so that you lose. Let me explain this:

1. The monsters never stop levelling up. Your buildings however have a max level. Therefore there will be a time (and it's not gonna take long) where the monsters overlevel your buildings (and keep on levelling up!). It doesn't even matter how many towers you build, after some time they will be so far ahead that you do 0 damage to them.

2. The corruption spreads, the more you play until it covers the entire map. The more it spreads, the more enemies get spawned. So that means you gotta fight it back right? No. If you fight it back, the game becomes more difficult. So you fight it back to make the game easier, but the game becomes harder instead. But even if you don't fight it back, you're in the way remember? Therefore once it reaches your city, then you are unavoidably fighting it back by simply existing lol. Therefore the game becomes even harder.

3. There is one way to win a map. To do nothing but head to the corruption immediately. When you remove it from the last tile, it won't spawn any monsters. This is more of an exploit than a design though, and if you do that it becomes clear why the dev didn't want you to win. Because that's it. Once you are able to play the game freely, there's nothing to it. Everything is geared towards protecting yourself from the monsters, and defending. So once you do that, the game has nothing else to offer. But read my previous points: the formula of the game is to make you lose. So there's no point in even defending then.

4. You can move your people nomadically to other tiles on the world map. Therefore you might assume that the point is defending and gather resources, move elsewhere, gather more resources, move elsewhere etc, until you're tough enough to start actually fighting the corruption. No. That would make the game cool actually. But that's not its point. Because remember, no matter how many resources you have, the enemies do not have a max level, therefore will always overpower you. Even if we imagined you have infinite resources, your towers at some point will do no damage.

5. TD element. The game initially had this, and it was great. Basically you were supposed to build a maze of towers. That's why there are also slow towers and stuff like that. The enemies would not attack walls unless they had no way of reaching your town. But after some update, the monsters would start attacking the walls anyway, therefore negating this completely. So in the end, you're stuck with towers that's counter-productive to build. Why have a slow tower, if you could build another elemental/arrow/ballista tower? There's no point.

6. God powers. Initially, they matter. But after a while, they are so weak that you are stuck with casting stuff like regenerating resources - mainly food. Also, charm, if I remember, you can take any enemy under your command. So to win, reach the corruption fast, then when a high level fire elemental is spawned, charm it. Do that until you remove the last tile. 

7. Upgrading God powers: So you can upgrade certain stuff by mainly doing stuff in the game. These are the "goals", and it can increase your max levels and stuff. Wonderful huh? Therefore, you can at some point overpower the enemies, right? No. We already talked about how enemies' levels are infinite. By finishing a goal, you will, like, upgarde the level of something by 1. Golems if I remember. One level doesn't mean much. The enemies by then will probably be 10 levels ahead already, if you're lucky.

8. The dev doesn't care about these problems. It's been posted time and time again that the game has no purpose, as it's designed so that you lose. Everyone says this. I went to the comments just now to see if anything changed, and I found a comment from 1 hour ago that says the game is unfair etc.

Look, I don't want an easy game, by no means. I'm happy with a challenge, even if I lose, because then I know more stuff so I can replay and be better. But this isn't a challenge. This is a losing simulator. Actually, what will happen is that you will replay and replay, and at some point you will realize my previous points and give up, because there is no way to win the game.

And just as you're thinking the dev is gonna take notice and do this game justice, they release it from Early Access without "fixing" anything. And I use quotes because I don't think the dev sees these as problems, I really think the dev wanted the game to be impossible. But I don't know why, this game could be cool. Please remember, and I'll say this again and again, your skill doesn't matter. This isn't a "git gud" scenario. You will lose every time because that's how the game is designed.

So anyway, yeah, my advice is to steer clear of this game unless for some reason you really want to lose.

Then contain spawns with a couple of bullet towers while you rush town growth to supporting a bunch of crystal golems. Once that's ready slowly light creep into the corruption area until it's all gone.

Enemy strength increases exponentially over time and with corruption size, so containing it ASAP is basically the only way to win.  Towers are useless beyond the first few in-game weeks and human military is too hard to replace so there's no real other options on offense either.

This is a literal trash game. More than one hundred hours spent and I would not recommend. What went wrong? 

Let's start with the positives. The developer is very sympathetic and has produced technically impressive results for the one-man studio. The game has received a lot of attention and updates are still frequent. It is a game that I'd love to like. All the basic building blocks are solidly done.

Yet there is something wrong on a fundamental level.

Core design idea for the game was that you couldn't win it. You're meant to literally "rise to ruins", i.e. you are fighting to lose as effectively as you can. In some games, like Dwarf Fortress, losing can be fun. A spectacular failure from the player's side leads to a death spiral where the game ends.

But in RtR you don't have that much fun losing. You don't feel like you lost because you (or your virtual villagers) did something particularly stupid. 

Every day the night comes and with every night come increasingly stronger monsters. Recovering from failures is extremely difficult. You lose because you are meant to lose, you lose because somewhere along the line you did a sub-optimal design choice. Or you lose because you failed to micro a strong enemy that your defenses couldn't handle.

The idea of spending tens of hours on building a village to lose didn't sit too well with the players, so the developer grudgingly added the possibility for winning the map by eliminating corruption. You achieve this by turtling down, building campfires to blockade the corruption into a fraction of the map. And eventually pushing it back. 

Every day the enemy gets stronger. This is done by simply bloating the numbers. So you end up having a long game where the enemy soon has thousands of hitpoints on a single unit. Meanwhile, your defenses stop improving, and your villagers have a limited lifetime. Soon it reaches the point where the only effective way to remove a strong enemy is to manually pick it up and throw it into a magical furnace.

As the corruption strength grows, even a single tile of corruption will be able to spawn hundreds of enemies that all can wipe out your entire defenses if they get through. Combine this with the fact that corruption can live inside mountains, and enemies can spawn from inside of said mountains...

Talking about enemies getting through defenses, we have to talk about the trash in the game. One of the most idiotic additions to the game were the trash mechanics. Every industry in the game has a chance of producing trash. If left alone, trash spawns slime monsters.

So players have to build buildings to store and process the trash. Soon you have to dedicate a very sizeable population of your village for trash management: carrying trash from one place to another. Even though you have many different ways for disposing of trash, they all take a long time to process it. So in practice, you start having more and more trash piled up.
Now, if a single enemy manages to destroy a building (which in late game they can do in seconds), the destruction releases a torrent of trash that needs to be dealt with. Due to your trash starting to pile up, you find yourself frequently losing buildings to trash slimes. And eventually, a slime will destroy a junkyard.

So now imagine your village that you've painstakingly built and fought hard for, dying to a trash spiral. Once trash hits a certain number, there simply is no way to dispose of it fast enough. You might have a village of hundreds of villagers, yet they simply are not fast enough in rebuilding junkyards and hauling the trash.

You are playing a literal god who can throw meteors and summon earthquakes. Yet you have no way of getting rid of common garbage.

Even if we forgive trash mechanics and trash design with number bloat, there is one thing a town builder/tower defense game cannot be forgiven for. And unfortunately, RtR also fails on that front.

The defense part of the game is uninspired and not much fun. You can build various defensive towers that shoot at the enemy, buildings that spawn defensive unit and different types of walls. That is it. Most of the walls and tower types are not really usable, so your options are even more limited.

No environmental interactions are possible. You can drown a fire elemental by dropping it into the water, but you can't flood a maze. No Dwarf Fortress-like mechanical contraptions, no physical traps.

Enemies are the same kind of zombies, skeletons, ghosts and slimes. They just get more hitpoints. Every enemy is tiny and hard to see, especially with magic and other effects going on.

Frankly, the defense part of the game is a chore that you will soon be dreading. Since your defenses are ineffective, you are forced to personally micromanage the tiny enemies, picking them up and dropping them, or occasionally smiting them with your god powers. And every night this becomes more and more annoying. Just like the game itself.

So, in summary. An impressive effort that is ruined by poorly thought design choices. Unless future updates radically alter the core philosophy of the game, I really don't see the game being salvageable. Ask yourself if you like games where losing a slow and tedious death is mandatory before making your purchase.

I really want to like this game, but it has too many bizarre shortcomings to work for me. The clever art style, the overall "goal" and the hybrid RTS/city builder/tower defense should combine to be a ton of fun. However, this game is probably best described as a frustration simulator; a steep difficulty curve, a relentless enemy AI, and your greatest obstacle- arguably the worst pathing/friendly AI ever coded join forces to waste your time. Your best winning strategies means nothing, as your builders will disregard your build orders, obvious pathing routes, and will even starve to death rather than survive even when food is readily available. Priorities you the player set are flatly ignored. Builders wander into enemy territory to be slaughtered without reason at least once every scenario, losing more than 2 or so is debilitating to your economy, and you're quickly overrun. Your towers and defense systems target priority is laughable, and there is no means for the player to directly control any of this to fill the gulf in logic between what is happening and what the AI thinks it should be doing. I would compare it to another game, but I genuinely can't think of any game in any of the genres Rise to Ruins taps into that relies so heavily on micromanagement that then leaves it entirely to an AI that is, at it's very best, incompetent. Credit where it's due, Rise To Ruins is a beautiful looking game, and it's clear the developer(s) put a lot of heart into the final product- I don't feel this game is "broken" for lack of effort on their part. 

Granted you're the sort who doesn't mind having to restart your scenario every 2 hours or so because your villagers all decided to wander into harms way for no apparent reason (as there's only one save slot per map per difficulty, so no quicksaving!) then this game may just be your cup of tea. If you (like me) prefer a strategy game where you are actually in "control" and not just shouting suggestions at a dimwitted AI, then Rise to Ruins is best skipped over.

It's sad, but after many dozens of hours, I have to conclude that Rise of Ruins, in its current "finished" state, is just... not that fun to play.

For starters, it's poorly balanced. The tower defence elements spoken of in the game's description are essentially optional for the most part; far better is to use walls and towers only while you have no other option, then plonk a bunch of golem creation stations, upgrade them fully, make sure they have the more useful elements (cold is good because fire elementals are a massive pain; poison is crap because slimes and zombies resist it) and then go do whatever you feel like until you get really, really bored.

The golems go off to fight the enemy, some golems die, they get replaced from the golem combobulator structure, and your village and people are safe as long as your golem output exceeds your losses in battle.

Meanwhile, if you build a wall maze and a bunch of towers? Monsters will run past (or shoot over, i.e. fire elementals), smash up your buildings, and your starting bunch of builders will have to stop building up your infrastructure in order to fix the half-smashed buildings, lest they be fully ruined. Some villagers die.
If you want, you can get some villagers to act as "rangers" if you build a place for them, which mostly means they'll more often try to fight instead of running away from monsters. That can work pretty well against basic early-game enemies; not so much against fire elementals who have a powerful ranged attack, or spectres who resist physical damage. If you were thinking you could have your smith craft some magical bows or swords to even the odds, nope. Mundane weapon crafting only, and so much gear drops from killed monsters that I never feel the need to produce it, even if it wasn't mostly useless in the first place. So you make golems instead.

All of which is a shame, as the towers are pretty varied and interesting. They just don't work very well. You have to supply two types of ammunition depending on the tower type, and/or magical energy that requires you to build a sort of mana collector. Meanwhile, golems cost some energy too, but by the time you can upgrade the golem buildings, you'll be producing "crylithium", refined crystals that can be shoved in a mana collector to generate mana out of nowhere. Yeah, they call it influence or energy, I know, but really, it's mana.

So, the combat/strategy is not so much about adapting to situations or trying different models, as it is about doing the exact same thing every time. Not great for a game with a wide selection of large maps to its "world"/campaign mode... the changes of scenery are nice, but happen pretty rarely unless you start off at the corner of three different environment types on the world map, and even then... an in-game year is maybe 40-ish days, and you have to survive for a year on each map to win the campaign, seemingly? Which doesn't sound so bad until you realize a day in this game takes what feels like an hour or more, in real time. There are options to increase the game speed, which helps a little, but not enough.

The forces of evil in this game are confusing, too. They start off roughly opposite wherever you start your own colony, on each map. Then they claim territory by "corrupting" it. But if you just leave them alone and let them claim, say, half the map? They don't even seem to bother you much. A few monsters will wander in to attack your place, but as long as you can get a chain of bonfires splitting your half of the map off from theirs (which isn't that difficult), you'll probably be fine. Apparently crowding the enemy into a corner will drive them into a more hostile mode, but from what I can recall, that didn't pose much difficulty either. So you have this peculiar situation where the living dead and the... cultists, or whatever, who for some reason have Borg names (Seven of Nine, and similar), and flame creatures that like to burn people alive, are all part of a weird ecosystem which you're supposed to view as some kind of natural balance? A neat idea on some levels, but in the end, your golems will stomp all over anything that tries to cross your bonfire line, and the whole thing ends up being a weird ancillary feature, even though it was added fairly recently IIRC.

Then there's the civilian economy. I used to enjoy this, but it too gets very repetitive once you've learned the ropes. Make sure you have enough people growing food, collecting, purifying and bottling water, and harvesting wood and stone and crystal and whatever else you need. Have one or two people making boards and cutting stone blocks. Balance the number of builders and porters ("organizers"). Build a clinic to reduce the chances of a miscarriage as your villagers procreate. Keep building enough housing to attract nomads, increasing your population. It's all more of a hassle than a joy, to be honest, and once you've got everything running smoothly, it's all just sort of... there. And you sit and wait for the days to slowly roll by behind your wall of shooty golems (or your wall of stone and towers if you want to be a rebel)... days and nights pass, seasons shift, and there's still not much to do beyond upgrading things gradually and maybe building more homes.

This is all at Survival difficulty, by the way... Nightmare may offer more of a challenge for those familiar with the gameplay, but the thing is, to switch to that, one would have to start a new world, and after playing most of a year on just one map, I'm just not up for that. Mind-numbing does not begin to describe it.

As a sort of god-like entity, you have various spells/miracles available to you. You can't use any of them on corrupted territory, but some have a wide area of effect and could be invoked on nearby uncorrupted ground, so there is that. I like being able to call down a thunder storm and maybe fry a few enemies, with the weather changing to rain as the primary effect. It's nice to have a spell that makes trees, crystals and wild-growing vegetables grow. The grabby hand spell lets you dump fire elementals in lakes, which is brilliant, but you'll mostly use it to pull rocks off mountains and maybe drop them on building sites when you don't have much workforce to go around... and then you have to recharge your mana, because the grab spell consumes some with each pickup, and drains it every second you're holding something. Mana comes from many sources, which is kind of neat, but gathering it soon becomes just another chore. In addition to the aforementioned and a few other nice options, there are also various less meaningful spells that mostly feel like filler, of little to no use even early on in the game. There's nothing remotely as cool as the spells in Populous 3, to use a classic example; no volcano, no seeking fire blast, no tornado, no land bridge/ramp spell.

What else? Well, marking resources and adjusting buildings' operational parameters is a chore. Managing your workforce is a chore. Migrating to a new region is a much bigger hassle than it was back in Early Access, when you could just whisk people up into stasis with a spell that is now gone, and then settle them anywhere you jolly well please; now you have to build a migration station, a courier station, set how many people to move to one of the adjacent regions, wait for them to gather, wait for them to leave, ship necessary goods along with them... I dunno, maybe someone thinks all that sounds fun. If so, this may be the game for you!

There is also a strange system of very gradually earned minor bonuses on the world map which begs the question, "Is the game supposed to get easier and easier after the first map?" What you really need is a bonus that makes the days pass faster. Better still, if all there is to this game is to build all the things (in the "right" order of course) and then wait ages for the victory clock to tick over... why play it at all?

Rise to Ruins is a fairly brutal village building god game, if played as intended. In fact its basically quite unfair, and the game pulls lots of tricks to ruin your village and any fun you're having building a village. There are thankfully modes of incremental difficulty for the less masochistic gamers, and the core difficulty curve can be learned in relative safety in a Traditional Mode. The issue is village AI is fairly dumb, and you have no control over them except in an obtuse sense. Villagers will walk into enemy land while "wandering" outside of the village, starve to death with a massive surplus of food, and generally bug out and not do their job even if you have set up everything to be as efficient as possible. And this is working as intended, apparently.

You build a little pixel village under threat from a spreading corruption that decays the land and spawns bad guys. You are a deity with a fairly comprehensive set of powers, both destructive, creative, healing, and utility in nature. You have no influence over land that is corrupted, so cannot attack it directly, and for the most part the corruption cannot be conquered or destroyed, only endured. The point of the game is to simply survive for as long as possible, through defenses and arming of your villagers and judicious use of magic. 

There is an overworld map, and each region on the overworld is a biome to survive in. The only primary victory condition is to survive a year in every region, which you have to spread to organically from each village you form via migrating villagers you select to leave for the new region.

And that is Rise to Ruins. You are a deity to a small group of people trying to simply survive an unstoppable, albeit partially containable, corruption. If you enjoy god games and village builders, and a have a taste for lite tower defense, this is a very fun and addicting game. Be warned, on Survival and higher difficulties it can be brutal, and even on Traditional difficulty a few too many mistakes and setbacks late into a village can doom it. There are many "features" to enemy AI that will essentially ignore established rules to circumvent your defenses, and added to this are "random" disasters like earthquakes and lighting storms that target your village. Pretend its just the corruptions angry god throwing its own spells at you if it helps justify it.

How to say this? I was having incredible fun until I encountered a new, recent, apparently purposefully implemented mechanic that utterly destroys the game. I wish I played it before this new mechanic as the game would have been perfect before it.

Basically, the game tells you that you can build a maze to protect your base and that monsters don't destroy walls, aka your typical "tower defense" game. Combined with being a village simulator, the fun is tremendous at first. All seems perfect whilst you're being hooked into the game, building up your maze, defenses, and base whilst racing against the clock of increasing zombie presence. What's not to love? That is until the game dumps a giant "gotcha" on you that ruins everything. Any player would think you can build your own maze and defense towers to protect your village exactly as described - this is how the game advertises itself after all. Not anymore thank to this new shitty mechanic I mentioned.

I realized the hard way that if enough monsters are present, or your maze is complicated enough (and eventually one of these two things must happen given the increasing difficulty in monster attacks) then the monsters will simply destroy your walls, ignoring your maze completely to destroy your village. This going completely against what you're taught in the beginning tooltip. Inevitably, your days-long deeply designed and beautiful maze will become utterly useless and pointless. 
All this happens even after you religiously follow the guidance from the tooltips that "monsters must have a path to your base or else they will destroy  walls". It doesn't matter if they have a path. Even if they do and you follow what you're taught from the tutorial religiously, the monsters will eventually decide to destroy your walls and ignore your maze anyway, taking you completely by surprise.

It would be fine being defeated if the monsters managed to make it through your maze, but if they can't get through it, they instead ignore it and simply "win anyway" by breaking your walls. This doesn't happen until the ultra-late game when you least expect it, and when you've finally designed a grand, but ultimately worthless and useless maze.

This new mechanic of zombies destroying walls apparently didn't use to exist. The developer thought it "fun" to add it. I'm not the only one to have complained about it. The only way I can sum up this game, is it's like eating a delicious looking chocolate cake that entices all your senses, only for you to realize that it was baked with salt instead of sugar once it melts in your mouth. 

And to think the developer purposefully implemented this mechanic to make the game "more difficult". How about just letting your players play the game to have fun with mechanics that they're taught to be aware of without an ultra late-game "gotcha" that completely defeats the entire purpose of playing in the first place?

Caveats: I realize building double, triple or even thicker layer walls supposedly mitigates this problem (but it doesn't prevent it). It's not a solution due to 2 reasons - 
1) Building a huge single tile thick Curtain Wall takes literally days in real life due to the inordinate resource requirements (every Curtain Wall block requires special refined stone as opposed to ordinary stone).  If you're building a complex maze, a single-tile thickness maze is already exhausting enough. Doubling or tripling the time required to increase wall thickness just to avoid this "new mechanic" whilst also fighting against increasing monster spawns is the very antithesis of what a game should be about.
2) Even if you did do the above, eventually as the monster spawn rates increase enough your walls will STILL be broken down anyway, no matter how many tiles thick they are. All you're doing is delaying how long it takes. Apparently if there are enough monsters, they will reach a threshold to break your walls. All you're doing by doublng, trippling, quadrippling etc. the thickness requirement is simply delaying the fact that the monsters can still break down the walls anyway if there are enough present, OR if your maze is too complex. And it's not as if the game can't handle complex mazes, as I said, this is an apparently recently implemented mechanic!

This game is a classic example of a fantastic idea, with a seemingly fantastic dev, completely ruined by over tampering and "improvement", like many games before it. I wish I could have played this game before this new mechanic. It would have been great fun building mazes to defend your base. A pity the game has taken a direction where this isn't what it wants to be anymore, and gives you no hint about that whilst you're playing. You will only realize your maze is worthless in the ultra-late game when you need it most and have finally finished building it.

TL;DR: A perfect game, utterly ruined for no reason due to dev over-tampering.

Mostly at night. You transition to a tower defense game, constructing towers and golems to fight the enemy, weaving a maze of walls for the enemy to traverse, holding strong as your villagers cower and attempt to reinforce every defense while balancing seasonal survival needs. This is all very cool... until it's not. 

You WANT to send out a force to counter-attack the enemy base camps. The game isn't designed for that. You WANT to eradicate the threat from every sector of the World Map one by one. But again, that’s not what this game is about. The best you can do is... survive. For awhile. And then die. Yes, you can play on more peaceful settings, but you miss out on the tension which, early on, is really very good. Here, in Rise to Ruins, you grow until your villagers are defeated, with goals like "Survive 21 days!" as your only incentive to keep going. All defense and no offense creates an artificial limit on what this game COULD be. The potential is there, but ultimately it's a bust for me. Sigh. Rise to Ruins is a cross between a city builder and tower defense game. You build a city during the day, and at night enemies attack you. You have to build towers and walls to kill the enemies before they enter your base and start wreaking havok.

In the campaign, the world map is divided into regions. You pick one region as your starting region, and build your first city there. To conquer that region, you need to survive there a year. Then you can send people and resources to other regions to begin again there. The catch: The game stage progresses for all regions at the same rate, so when you start that next region, you will almost immediately be assaulted by top-level troops. If you haven't sent enough people and supplies to get defenses built by the end of the day, you're screwed. But, you are limited on how much you can send to a region in one day, so the longer you take to send things, the more difficult the game gets. You can unlock bonuses to help you combat the difficulty, but the slow rate that the game runs at essentially guarantees that you would have to spend the next 30 years playing to win the game. Not really my idea of fun.

Besides this, my other biggest complaint is the garbage collection. As your people work, they generate garbage which has to be collected and stored or burned. This is a pain in the rear. Who in the world thought it was a good idea to introduce garbage collection (including Wall-E bots) in a medieval fantasy city builder? No thanks. 

Before the garbage collection mechanics were added, I would have given this game a thumbs-up for single-scenario play, just to see how long you could survive, ignoring the campaign altogether. Now, I have to give it a thumbs down overall.

This game is getting a lot of consistent work and polish, and I appreciate it, but it still falls into a major category of frustrating that I can't seem to get over, and that is that villagers, that backbone of your economy are complete idiots.

Builder is the default worker position, where the job assignment for the villager is "go get whatever is needed to build the building that is on the top of the builder priority list." It's not extremely efficient role but it's very versatile and useful, especially at the beginning of the game. However, if you have built too many buildings, they just... stop functioning; they get stupid and stand around like brain-damaged penguins. in the meantime, your town gets overrun.

If I decide to add 30 building plans to my town, let me do that. Don't have the game punish me for ambitiously planning ahead of what my town is going to look like. The builders don't need to drop everything, they can just finish what they were doing and move onto the next thing when they are done.

"That's not how the game is played!"

That's how I'm playing the game. If it doesn't let me play that way, I'm gonna stop playing, and this review will stay red.

Edit: Years in, achievements have been added, and villagers are still brain-damaged penguins. I spend more time dragging single resources to buildings and dropping monsters into sacrifice pits than I do playing an actual game. It's not compelling gameplay. This is a simulator desperately in search of a game. It's sad too, because if the villagers weren't phenomenally stupid, this wouldn't feel like such a slog.

The reason I wouldn't recommend this game can be condensed into the following sentence: Rise to Ruins is not a game you win.

That's not to say it's especially difficult, or it has an unreasonable learning curve, or anything like that; it's that the game is literally not designed for you to "win" it; the devs have admitted as much in a post on the Steam forums.

The game's "enemy" (for lack of a better term) is "The Blight", which is this area of dark, diseased ground on each village map that spawns monsters. As time goes by in the village, the Blight spreads and spawns more monsters. You can hold the Blight at bay or even push it back by building structures next to it, but that doesn't weaken it; it actually makes it "angry" and causes it to spawn more monsters. The more time goes by, the stronger the Blight becomes. There is no way to weaken it, so, eventually, no matter how well you defend yourself, you will be overcome.

You may ask "So what's the point of the game, then?". Well, the point is to establish a village, set up defenses, grow the population, create harvesting, refining, and production chains, and then take all your excess people and resources and move them to a new village sector before you're overcome by the Blight. Once in the new village, rinse and repeat.

There is no stage at which you grow so powerful and well established that you dominate the land and destroy the Blight. Eventually, given enough time, the Blight will consume you, and you will lose.

There isn't even a "passive" win state like in a Tycoon sim wherein you've built up your city/business/factory/amusement park/whatever to its ultimate potential and can then kick back and admire it. The Blight and monsters are still there, and they will still reduce all you've built to rubble.

In essence, Rise of Ruins isn't about "winning", it's about "accomplishing as much as possible before losing".

I'm not averse to grinding at a challenging game until I've finally won it, and I have over 500 hours in XCOM: Long War to prove it, but if I literally can't win because the game wasn't designed to let you win, I don't see the point.

Years on and it's still awful. Goodness knows I've tried putting up with it, but the villagers are dumber than the rocks they won't harvest no matter how hard you throw them at a cliff. I watched them complain about housing while I had six homes waiting to be built, missing logs, while I had over 150 units of the stuff stockpiled and gathering dust, with my builders just wandering around aimlessly.

For ten days.

Sometimes three farms produces enough food for twenty villagers, other times four doesn't produce enough for ten.

Villagers run away at the first sign of enemies, no matter how heavily armed and armored they are, which isn't the most helpful thing ever when they get outnumbered by slimes on day 2.

The AI, such as it is, seems to have two different settings: pretend to work, and gleefully do jack.

"Prepare to lose often!" works with games like Dwarf Fortress, because in DF the game is legitimately difficult. In Rise to Ruin, losing happens because nobody does any freaking work, and slapping a "game hurd tho!" label on it doesn't excuse crap programming.

Give it a chance if you like, but be ready to spend a lot of time waiting for your dozen builders to decide they feel like repairing the damage done to that house a week ago, or boggle as to why your maintenance and repair guy is delivering iron ingots to the toolmaker instead of fixing the sixteen forty damaged buildings you built the damn Maintenance post specifically to get someone to fix the freaking things.

In practice, the game is utterly bloated. You need three or four buildings just to make one operational (magic turret? need an energy collector, which needs to be powered from another building, which needs...), and the workers in those buildings do whatever they feel like, which is usually 'nothing whatsoever'. Got three people working in the lumber mill making wooden boards? Well, that one guy there is bringing logs from the lumber shack to the village center while you've got four buildings waiting for boards. So fun! Not like you need those boards to repel the endless army of weak monsters that will utterly destroy everything in sight while everybody runs away, so you can avoid losing on day 2! LOSING IS FUN, DO YOU GET IT YET?

It could be an amazing game with some actual effort put in, but a Decision(tm) was made a long time ago, when the game changed its name, and it has seemingly been downhill from there. The coding is like the workers themselves: it does whatever it feels like doing, which is usually nothing. I promise this is true: exiting the game and restarting it once caused all the workers to suddenly realise that they had jobs to do, and that game almost went well... for a few minutes. Restarting hasn't worked since; I think the code found the 'Make things go' exploit and patched it out.

The game is supposed to be challenging and unforgiving and I suspect that it's inspired by the idea of *fun* in Dwarf Fortress. Rise to Ruins is not fun, in the DF sense, at all. The reason DF is fun when you loose, often without any fault of your own, is that each loss tells a story which can be quite complex and nuanced.
Losing in Rise to Ruins was not fun at all as it just felt like I didn't manage the town well enough and no interesting story was being told. The game also doesn't tell you how to lose. You are probably supposed to just leave the region and reset the whole world if you lose but the game doesn't tell you this and just says that you are loosing all your progress by resetting the world.
The game is unforgiving in the worst of ways. I made the mistake of not preventing some corruption from entering a relatively thin strip of rock and the next thing I know, a very hard to reach part of a mountain had been corrupted. It would have been no effort at all to prevent this from happening but after it happened, It was going to take many hours to clean the corruption out of there. So I had a very successful town with a strong defense system practically ruined by not knowing the precise mechanics of the game, I didn't realize corruption went through rocks. Unforgiving punishments can be good game design but harsh punishments for rules that aren't explained nor obvious is not. 

I also think the game needs to be proofread. There are many strange sounding sentences like "Such a real shame." when someone dies.

I realize that It's just made by one guy but that doesn't make the game better or worse, it just explains why it is how it is.

Gameplay:
You pick a piece of land from a world map. Then you place your keep and drop some villagers and start collection ressources to build your town.
Most of the nights you are attacked by monsters and therefore have to build defenses.
The monsters spawn in a randomly placed piece of land labeld as corruption.
The wave of enemys get stronger and stronger and after 15 nights (the first year) you will loose due to massive power increase the monsters have.


Problems / bugs:
The game is not late game optimized. The longer the game runs and the bigger your town gets all the functions are breaking appart. Sometimes it takes a full morning just to build one building but you have 20 workers and full ressouces.

Building cheap bow towers is only for good for the first nights, because the more towers you have your AI will not be able to supply them with arrows. This is clearly a bug. I had 10 bow towers and two fully developed bowyers, they refuse to do anything.

Corruption spawns always the same amount of monsters regardless how big their town / area is. I attacked them early and nearly surrounded their spawn. I drove the corruption on the ground back. They only had one graveyard and 5 towers but they spawn the same amount like owning 20 graveyards.

You can not win on any map. You can not win against corruption. Neither by destroying their spawn nore by digging in and defending. Why? Because rebuilding the destroyed buildings takes too long. You just don´t have enough time to rebuild until the next night arrives. Maybe you manage to rebuild but next wave it stronger. You can´t win the arms race. Also if you dig in you will run out of stone and then you can not rebuild. So you must expend.
And destroying the spawn is impossible because building your town and reaching the spawn and building towers to defend just takes the first full year.

Once winter hits, it is game over.

Waymakers take way too long to build a path. Towers build a lot faster compared to a a stupid tile of path.

Ressource transport takes way too long if you base is far away from the building place.
(This is rediclious: You must expend to contain the corruption, but you can´t expend because your logistics fail, even with 25 workers running day and night).

In late game (day 15+) your golems just die so quickly to the enemy. The only golums that are useful are crystal golems because of their range attack. The wood and stone golems get eaten up.

No focus fire. In late game the enemy sends "fire golems" they will attack from range and burn your towers from save distance. You can not take them out by focus fire, because there is no focus fire. And your towers will always attack nearst target not "Target with highest priority". Even if your defense is able to hold of the wave these fire golems will kill some of your towers and you can´t rebuild in time.

You can´t attack corruption. During daytime i outnumber the enemy. I have 40 golems and turrets, during nighttime enemy sends 100 monsters. GG. Why can you not send your army of soldiers and golems to attack the corrution? Why do you even allow the monsters to build turrets? Monsters dont have to defend their base because you can´t even attack. LOL.

I love this game. At the start of development it seemed like a great way to look at an escalating defense game. It is not fun worrying about if my people are getting their back scratched correctly. I am defending them from death on the other side of thin wall. At any moment an earthquake could take out everything these little people built, and I protect, away with the help of the hoards of monsters outside.

Pros: It is a difficult base building game where you have to defend against increasingly harder to kill enemies. There are specialized towers to help you with this that each have their purpose. You can build nearly anywhere and eventually create a happy nook of salvation until eventually time takes your kingdom into ruins. You have to care and provide for your people so they can survive and proliferate. There is a bit of a learning curve, but your bonuses carry over to the next run.

Cons: The direction the game is currently headed is not focusing on the death on the outside of your little shelter, it is currently focused on making the game a little bit of nitpicking and making sure your people get their back scratched the correct direction. The game is already difficult with the 100% random events that can end your run at any moment but you will have to worry about their trash, and toiletries. I can't really recommend this game. It has some issues that probably won't ever get fixed.
The bad:
- Abandonment: The game is likely abandoned at this point. According to Steamdb, it had only three updates in the past three years: two bug fixes and the achievement update.
- Lack of Campaign and Poor Progression: The lack of a campaign and the fact that every building is unlocked from the start take away from the enjoyment of learning about the world and discovering new things. The only progression comes in the form of chests that you unlock with points earned during gameplay. These chests provide minor bonuses, such as one extra building slot, but most of them are percentage increases to stats. And they are all capped so you cannon end up having 1000 extra building slots.
- Unintuitive UI: The UI is not very user-friendly. It has large elements on all four sides of the screen, which are fixed in size and only scalable to a limited extent. On my 22-inch 1080p monitor, the text is too small. Scaling the UI makes the text bigger, but it also hides more of the screen. The game itself warns that changing the scale may cause visual issues, which is not a good sign. I've calculated that about ~24% of the screen is occupied by the UI at 1x scale.
- Missing Game Features:
  * If you accidentally start deleting a building, there is no way to stop it. Since dismantling isn't instant and villagers have to perform it, there should be an option to cancel the process.
  * You cannot rotate buildings. This is problematic as it limits the way you can design your town. Only rectangular buildings need both vertical and horizontal sprites; square ones can remain as they are.  I read on some posts that the artist would have to make new sprites for each build. I can understand that this would be time-consuming but it really messes with the game
- Lack of Clarity: The game is generally not very clear. The in-game tutorial only covers the basics. I often had to search online for answers, which led me to old posts, some as old as five years, where the developers provided responses. However, these answers might be outdated now.
- No Endgame: There is no endgame content. You just play a series of skirmish battles with the same buildings, fighting the same enemies on different maps. The goal of each map is to survive for one year. The difficulty settings seem to only increase the enemies' aggression.

The good:
- I like the music.
- The pixel art and particle effects are very nice.

100 hour review:

For a city builder the AI is weak. You can't control their behavior, schedule their work, restrict zones, lock gates, assign food or work policies, and can't control the villagers directly. Due to this the majority of the challenge mid to late game becomes preventing your villagers from constantly trying to wonder away from your village to pickup resources next to the enemy which is suicide. Workers can only build one thing at a time, if you have 100 units of wall sections and 100 builders you'd think it would be a quick job but no, they will ALL go towards one section and then in to a section thats furthest away.

The towers in this game are not balanced. Early game you can get by without them by picking up enemies and dropping them into a "cullis", its a building which instantly kills any thing thrown into it. Early game towers aren't necessary and late game they are pointless as mobs scale indefinitely and you don't.  When mobs scale to 15,000 health and 5x faster movement speed your tower that shoots for 30 when you first started the map is not going to do much. And one of the main utility towers called "banish tower", its projectile speed isn't even fast enough to catch the enemies passing next to it.

Strategy late game consists of 97% of you picking up enemies with 15,000 health(every single one of them and there are thousands of them each night) and dropping them into a cullis, because your 30-40 damage tower isn't going to get the job done. There are 5 type of enemies, 3 of which are susceptible to being permanently frozen, the other 2 types which are specters and fire elementals you would need to drop into a cullis and its not fun to do it few hundred times. The other 3% is remembering to recast your AOE freeze spell, don't do it too many times or your FPS will drop to single digits. Building a maze is optional, making the enemy funnel at a single point is sufficient for this strategy.

I've tried this game a few times over the last 6 months since I've purchased it.

It has a great concept.   I like the idea.   However, it's just a total fail when it comes to implementation.   The root of the problem is the absolutely WONKY AI when it comes to your village people. (Y M C A)   Its been brought up and mentioned to the dev numerous times in the forum and the response is "it works fine."

Let me describe the scenario:

1) You have a water purifier near a lake.  You have water masters harvest from the pond and bring  it back to the water purifier.   Attempting to turn dirty buckets of water into clean water.   While they are doing that, the farmer decides his crops need water and go to the water purifier to steal the dirty water to water his crops.   The water master gets pissed, goes back to the farm and steals the water buckets back.   The farmer then goes to the water purifier and steals the dirty water again... Repeat for eternity.  So in the end, all your guys are doing is swapping materials back and forth between buildings.

Same thing with every other resource.  I've seen it happen to wood, stone, etc.

The more buildings you have, the more the problem rears its ugly head.  You have more buildings and more citizens fighting over the resources.  As the game proceeds and you have 30+ buildings, the economy starts to crawl, and you start to notice nothing is actually being built very fast.   You start using your "hand of god" and plucking trees and dumping them on buildings to create them faster...  You see citizens wandering around, but you are now getting less than 1 building built per day.  When the game first starts off, you can build 10 buildings in the first day without much trouble.

2) With the new trash update, it seems the trash men like to pick up the corruption's garbage.  They will leave my town, which is walled in, to pick up some garbage outside of town and get picked off from corruption towers, and what not.   While they are out there being attacked, it triggers your golems to come to the defense of the town because "Buck Rodgers" went to clean up outside of the walls.  They die... So now during the day you are constantly chugging away your magic/mana/essence reviving golems and now you have to micro manage the garbage men and keep picking them up with your "hand of god" and dumping them back into town.

All in all, the game is great for about the first 10 days on the map.  After that the system breaks down and you get a buggy mess of frustration.  For that reason I cannot recommend the game.  However, if we can get the dev to work on a few of these issues this game could really be a rockstar.
